Hi All,

* <> *TL;DR*: Privacy won’t block the enablement of this feature in AZ, but it is not recommended unless there is a very strong business case for doing so. There would also be some edge cases that need to be addressed, especially from a CS perspective.

* From a Privacy perspective, there are less _direct_ risks — i.e. we would actually be collecting +_less_+ personal data in that some ‘Riders' wouldn’t register with us and download the app. 
* It is also important to note that our Privacy Notices *do not currently cover Street Hailing Riders* and because we never interact with them, we don’t show them this Privacy Notice or obtain their consent (if required by law). This means that if we ever collect or process Street Hailing Rider data, it would bring with it other compliance risks that would need to be addressed by us.
* As the enablement of this Feature is very recent, we don’t have a complete picture of ALL the issues that may arise. However, as we’ve seen in Dubai, enabling Street Hailing brings with it some compliance edge cases that would need to be covered - such as where a Street Hailing Rider loses a device during a Street Hailing trip and needs to contact CS and the Driver. Therefore, if the Team were to decide to enable it, Privacy would need to support the CS Team in AZ with an updated procedure when dealing with Street Hailing Riders who contact us.
* Of course, there are various other considerations to take into account, especially safety considerations and my view is that we shouldn’t be enabling this feature unless there is a real business need and strong business case to do so. 

Thanks.

Indeed, there’s opportunity to tweak in different eta/ls to obtain noise. And it’s useful to set them differently for different predictions:

* set minimal ls (even as constant) and large eta for cases like Driver (generally no trend, but sharp deviations)
* set larger ls for cases like in rider (where we have gradually deviating trends)

Potential solution is that we could try different combinations of parameters and fix them for a specific market (we can completely fix them as constants or give them some degree of freedom with {{TruncatedNormal}}).

* that using random variables vs not using them would give slightly different predictions and that using gp_rv can change intervals

To summarise our call today:

# *Consent is essential* *when utilising user location data for promotional purposes*, including geofencing on both Android and iOS platforms.
# *Privacy advises obtaining consent in all instances*, despite Apple permitting a limited number of notifications (20-30) without it. The division of responsibility between Apple and Bolt regarding these notifications remains unclear.
# Currently, *privacy still suggest to rely on consent when Bolt aims to send personalised “operational updates” based on user location*. For example, notifying users that Bolt is available when they arrive at a foreign airport or providing instructions for using Bolt in a specific area.
## *Rationale*: It can be easily argued that such updates may be perceived as promotional, particularly if they originate from a marketing (LCM) function.
## This topic requires further research to clearly outline the associated risks & if this can be avoided. Privacy can assist with this if marketing wishes to pursue it. *Please reach out re/ this separately.*
# *Consent should be obtained* *for a specific purpose* - such as sending users updates or instructions regarding Bolt's availability based on their location. We have flexibility in how we phrase the description of the purpose, it can be general, but still must be understandable for our users.
# There is *no need to obtain consent twice* - i.e. once for general geofencing and again for the “Traveling” category - *as long as the initial permission clearly states the purpose of using location data/geofencing for marketing purposes.*
## Privacy needs to review the permission wording to ensure its compliance with privacy law’s consent requirements.
# Users must have the ability to *opt out of geofencing/location-based marketing* easily. This process should be as straightforward as granting consent, such as a simple toggle in the app settings.
{panel}

The procedure I would like to see, if possible, is that firstly, we have much stronger filters for drivers requesting to delete their accounts. This should include Alfred or Tier 1 agents asking specifically why they want to delete their accounts and offering alternatives. Then if drivers really do want to delete accounts, we should allow a cooling off period of 1 to 3 months during which they will be able to reactivate their accounts. This should help prevent fraud attempts. 

Finally, after this period, deletion should be permanent, to ensure against fraud.

{code:sql}SELECT

        WHEN r.user__created_age_in_days BETWEEN 6 AND 10 THEN '2.6-10 days'

GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY etl.country_code, 2
LIMIT 1000

To summarize: 

* Fraudulent drivers *cannot* delete their accounts (ID failed blocks, T&C non-compliance, temporary suspensions - custom blocks) 
* Standard drivers *can* delete their accounts. 


Here we have this issue: 

Due to general misconception, most standard drivers think that they must delete their account for the following reasons:

* Changes (vehicle change - city change - category change)
* Phone number change or bank details change


Current CS procedure does not include any filters to sort this:
Drivers request deletion, Tier 1 sends the template found in the KB, 24 hours pass by, account is deleted.

This then increases the amount of deleted accounts from standard drivers who want to be reactivated shortly after deleting their accounts due to this misconception. 

*For the Paraguay market, we suggest:* 

* Tier 1 (or Alfred): Ask driver what's the reason for the account deletion before proceeding to identify the issue.
* If driver indicates they want to make changes on their account instead, follow the article according to the specific request. 
* If driver confirms they want to proceed with the deletion, follow the next step.

* *Damage and No Ride:* User reports damage, no ride planed or they wanted to use the car, but can't because of the damage and request refund. 
* *Damage and Ride:* User reports damage before the ride to make sure they haven’t cased it. 
* *Damage and Ride:* user disappointed by car state and want to be refunded. 
*  *Damage and Ride:*  user caused the damage and want to know the consequences 
* *3rd Party Accident:* User reports an accident, needs guidance on insurance and next steps. 

*Vehicle Functionality:*

* *Broken AC/Faulty Car:* User wants compensation due to vehicle malfunction impacting their ride.
* *Odd Noises:* User reports strange noises, may want a check-up or refund depending on severity.
* *Flat Tire:* User requests roadside assistance, clarification on repair costs, and/or compensation.
* *Dashboard Errors:* User is concerned about car's safety due to errors, may need assistance or a replacement car.

*Vehicle Cleanliness (Dirty, Smelly)*

* *No Ride:* User reported poor car's state, don’t want to use the car and may request a refund
*  *Ride:* User wants to know cleaning procedures or they want to get a refund for unpleasant experience 
* *Car Wash Reimbursement:* user cleaned the car and want to be reimbursed. 

*Operational Issues*

* *Car Replacement/Refund Delays:* User wants a replacement car and/or refund, frustrated with slow support.
* *Long Investigation:* User is dissatisfied with the length of an investigation, wants a faster resolution.
* *Pass/Package Issues & Overcharge:* User has issues with their pass/package (e.g., overcharge, unused time), wants a refund or adjustment.
* *Lack of Communication/Guidelines:* User is unhappy with lack of contact from CS or unclear instructions in the app.

DM offers performance related configuration for every of the 3 stages of data migration:

* dump 
{noformat}# Configuration arguments of the dump processing unit.
mydumpers:
  global:                            # The configuration name of the processing unit.
    threads: 4                       # The number of threads that access the upstream when the dump processing unit performs the precheck and exports data from the upstream database (4 by default)
    chunk-filesize: 64               # The size of the file generated by the dump processing unit (64 MB by default).
{noformat}
* load 
{noformat}loaders:
  global:                            # The configuration name of the processing unit.
    pool-size: 16                    # The number of threads that concurrently execute dumped SQL files in the load processing unit (16 by default). When multiple instances are migrating data to TiDB at the same time, slightly reduce the value according to the load.
{noformat}
* incremental replication
{noformat}syncers:
  global:                            # The configuration name of the processing unit.
    worker-count: 16                 # The number of concurrent threads that apply binlogs which have been transferred to the local (16 by default). Adjusting this parameter has no effect on the concurrency of upstream pull logs, but has a significant effect on the downstream database.
    batch: 100                       # The number of SQL statements in a transaction batch that the sync processing unit replicates to the downstream database (100 by default). Generally, it is recommended to set the value less than 500.
{noformat}

Also, additional steps like validation, also have parameters that may be adjusted 

{noformat}validators:
  global:                # Configuration name.
    # full: validates the data in each row is correct.
    # fast: validates whether the row is successfully migrated to the downstream.
    # none: does not validate the data.
    mode: full           # Possible values are "full", "fast", and "none". The default value is "none", which does not validate the data.
    worker-count: 4      # The number of validation workers in the background. The default value is 4.
    row-error-delay: 30m # If a row cannot pass the validation within the specified time, it will be marked as an error row. The default value is 30m, which means 30 minutes.
{noformat}


However, dump and load can’t be adjusted online, only in advance. Incremental replication part can be paused, adjusted and resumed.

Hey [~accountid:5b7beb46b8624857f09efff9] , apologies on the delay on my end. I’ve synced with [~accountid:712020:0b1ccfcb-3809-460a-88ab-c96985ba329a] (who is responsible for PY and ZA), and we have some concerns regarding this. From my POV, I don’t think it’s a deal-breaker, but I suggest thinking about those points, as they heavily influence user trust/and could be considered as unethical by some people/regulators.

*Some main points/risks for Bolt and how to mitigate them:*

* The dashcam app collects video footage (potentially biometric data), GPS data, and driver behavior metrics, all of which qualify as personal data under privacy laws. If Bolt only promotes the app and drivers install and use it independently, DTI is the data controller. If Bolt integrates the app into its platform or accesses collected data, Bolt could be considered a joint controller under privacy law, which imposes additional obligations, including transparency and accountability. We’ll need to renegotiate agreement later in case we consider integration.
* I saw you created a ticket for the contract with DTI, but it’d be very helpful if you could add all the relevant information on how the partnership will look like - will we promote them, how, etc.
* While DTI does not explicitly state that facial recognition is used, if the app analyzes video footage for driver behavior, there is a risk of biometric data processing (which requires consent in most scenarios). If internal-facing cameras record riders, this could pose severe privacy concerns, especially if Bolt has access to these recordings. It’d be hard to defend ourselves, especially in case we offer integration into our app.
* he driver scoring system evaluates speeding, hard braking, and stop sign compliance. If these scores are used for penalties, incentives, or suspensions, they could qualify as a prohibited automated decision under privacy law. I suggest reconsidering the use of this - maybe they can offer the drivers a version of their app without this? If DTI is integrated into Bolt, it might be that we won’t be able to have this, as such behavioural monitoring is extremely sensitive.
* Last but not least - Drivers may feel pressured to use the app, even if it is "optional," due to potential competitive disadvantages if others use it. Riders may feel uncomfortable knowing they are being recorded without clear safeguards. We need to think how do we cover transparency, guidelines to use DTI/what do we do if the riders disagree with being recorded, etc.

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Bolt is entering into a partnership contract with Renault (RCR).
** RCR wants to promote the use of its Dacia vehicles.
** Under the partnership, Bolt will communicate RCR’s promotional offer to its drivers (both individuals and fleets).
*** The offer includes financing options, discounts, and vouchers for Dacia vehicles such as Logan, Jogger, Sandero, Spring, and Duster.
** We'll use our app, email, and phone communication channels to promote the offer to our drivers and fleets.
*** However, Bolt will not be directly involved in the contracting process between RCR and the drivers who choose to take advantage of the offer​.
** RCR will collect and centralize GDPR consent from drivers/fleets that ask for offers on their landing page. This data will be shared with Bolt for contacting drivers and branding the cars to ensure soft-exclusivity.
* Contract is the same as what has previously been reviewed by legal team (including Liis Sok). 
** Apparently both parties are independent controllers.
** The only para that was not approved is as follows:
*** “_2.3 RCR will collect and centralize the GDPR consent of its partners for marketing communication purposes and use them for contacting, personalized offer, contracting etc._”
** Based on previous tickets:
*** [+LSS-42933+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-42933]
**** Ops confirmed “We are not sharing any data”. Liis therefore commented “_Since we are not sharing any personal data then I removed clause 2.3 from the Agreement… Bolt is not collecting any consents regarding this partnership and making data available to RCR. Also removed section 8 since you confirmed that no personal data is being shared regarding this partnership_”. Ops pushed back and said if we can live with the clauses as-is. Liss said clause 8 was fine (even though no data sharing). However, 23. should be removed, “_as we are taking the obligation to collect ‘consents’ and making them available to RCR… As this is short term cooperation then you can take the risk that the counterparty will oblige us to provide such consents but we are actually not able to fulfill this_.”
**** RCS then agreed to remove clause 2.3.
**** In Feb 2025, new arrangement was flagged. As part of this, Ops stated “_The contract will be the same, except there will ba a clause regarding them collecting GDPR agreements, because they will send us the details of the fleets that apply for their offer, in their landing page - this step is necessary to measure the success and results of the partnership_”.
*** [+LSS-47049+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-47049]
**** It seems that Gab is handling this in tandem. No delegation - I think this has been mistakenly escalated to both of us.
**** Gab has asked various Qs, but not yet answered.
*** [+LSS-42076+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-42076]
**** This is a ticket with GFT, which is closed.
**** in terms of data sharing, we are not sharing data with RCR. However, “_They will share with us the data of the ones who will sign as interested in the offer ( Name, surname, email address, mobile phone number, and VIN of the ordered and purchased vehicle)_”.
**** Liis said “_As we will only be receiving data from the counterparty, then I added light touch data protection clauses to the Agreement ... It is important to stipulate that any data which the counterparty will share with Bolt is undertaken on the grounds of a valid legal basis and have the indemnification clause in place._”
* Timeline to jump on this is short - offer already started and lasts until end of June.

+*ANALYSIS*+

* Agreement is here: [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1uh_fLGYAce62IQHWGxpMUUzBs8oxyyGH/edit|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1uh_fLGYAce62IQHWGxpMUUzBs8oxyyGH/edit|smart-link] 
** *Value*: Agreement value is 0, as mutually beneficial. However, importance business for Bolt. As such, we can permit the third-party agreement.
** *Role* *of* *parties*: Independent controllers (8.1).
*** Parties are required to comply with applicable data protection laws, which is good.
** *Countries*: Romania
*** Appears that no international data transfers will be taking place.
** *Services* / *purposes*: To measure the success of the partnership.
*** Also, possibility of Bolt reaching out to the drivers for branding. Ask about this.
*** No data processing annex. Not a requirement, but difficult to measure compliance / for record-keeping. As such, advisable to include.
** *Data* *subjects*: Bolt drivers and fleet owners.
** *Categories of data*: Name, surname, email address, mobile phone number, and VIN of the ordered / purchased vehicle.
** *Dataflows*: RCR will send Bolt the details of drivers / FOs who have reached out to RCR and expressed interest in the offer.
** *Duration of processing*: Not specified.
*** Agreement is valid until 30 June 2025.
** *Compliance*: N/A - Controller-to-controller
** *Data breaches*: Parties shall inform each other “_immediately_” of any personal data breaches related to performing the Agreement.
*** This is quite burdensome on Bolt. 
** *Audits*: No explicit clause.
** *Termination*: Bolt can withdraw the offer from the platform if there is no uptake / if RCR is in breach.
** *Liability*: No indemnity / liability re data protection breaches.
*** Neither party can transfer its obligations to another without prior written consent.
* Clause 2.3: “_RCR will collect and centralize the GDPR consent of its partners for marketing communication purposes and use them for contacting, personalized offer, contracting etc._”
** This seems fine in principle as Bolt is not on the hook. However, worth asking for some more context here.
* Overall, risk profile here is low risk. As such, proposed edits are good to have, but not as essential as with other agreements.
** We are receiving the data as a controller, and already have most of it regardless of RCR’s actions. As such, unlikely that drivers would take issue with this.
* Re the marketing, where we are emailing to legal entities then this is B2B. Where we are emailing drivers about a promotion from a third party, this is B2C, and it is unlikely that we could rely on soft opt-in here. As such, we need:
** Opt-in consent;
** Clear means of opting-out; and
** Clear identity of the sender.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Check the following:
** Any other third parties involved?
** If RCR lets Bolt knows about interested drivers, is Bolt then reaching out to those drivers for branding? What does this entail?
** If the list of personal data that I have correct?
** Any context behind clause 2.3
* Re the marketing, advise that we need to ensure opt-in consent has been obtained here.
** Check with Kost if there are any other quirks.
* An an ideal world, we would have the following:
** An Annex containing a summary of the data processing activities. 
** Requirements regarding security of data transfers.
** Revised clause on personal data breaches (48 hours, obligations to cooperate / fix it).
** Pro-Bolt indemnity. This is what I would push for the hardest.
* If time is short / amendments unlikely, we can accept the edits provided that the business is aware of the risks.

+*SUGGESTED APPROACH*+ :geo_map: 

Ordinarily, when personal data is being shared between Bolt and a third party (which for now I assume is still the case here), we would always push for the third party to enter into a full Data Sharing Agreement with Bolt - particularly given that the DSA would clearly define the scope of any data sharing (which the current Agreement does not). However, the risk profile here is lowered by the fact that Bolt is likely only the _recipient_ of any personal data. As such, *we can take a risk-based approach and proceed without a full Data Sharing Agreement*, given the tight timeline.

+*Nevertheless*+, as currently drafted, Clause 8 of the Agreement: (1) places unclear and overly burdensome obligations on Bolt; and (2) does not adequately protect Bolt’s position in the event that RCR breaches its data protection obligations. I have therefore included some amendments in suggesting mode, together with an explanation behind each amendment ([Link|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1uh_fLGYAce62IQHWGxpMUUzBs8oxyyGH/edit]). 

{color:#36b37e}*I would strongly recommend pushing for these amendments as a bare minimum*{color}, for the reasons set out in my comment bubbles. I have summarised these risks below.

{panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
*Risks of not including the amendments*

*(1) Unclear obligations*

* Since we are not including an overview in the Agreement of what personal data is being shared / for what purposes, it is important that we at least focus the scope of Clause 8 to _relevant_ data sharing activities. Otherwise, it is unclear what the obligations apply to (which would be a headache for Bolt if we ever had a dispute with RCR over data protection issues).

*(2) Liability for Bolt*

* Even though the parties are independent controllers and are individually accountable for their own compliance, Bolt could still be liable for RCR’s non-compliance with data protection requirements.
** If, for example, an error in RCR's systems resulted in the personal data at-issue being the subject of a data breach, it is possible that a disgruntled driver or fleet owner could pursue an action against Bolt (being the entity most readily available to the driver / fleet owner) for failing to keep their personal data safe.
* Without an indemnity in place, it would be difficult for Bolt to recover any losses resulting from such liability. This is therefore an extremely important provision to include.

*(3) Proportionate management of data breaches*

* As previously drafted, either party had to notify the other of a relevant personal data breach “immediately”. This would be burdensome on Bolt if we were the party that suffered the personal data breach.
* On the other hand, if an error in RCR's systems resulted in the personal data at-issue being the subject of a data breach, and we discovered that Bolt needed to notify the data protection regulators about this, we need to ensure that Clause 8 requires RCR to provide Bolt with enough information about the breach promptly. Otherwise, Bolt may not be able to notify the regulators in time, which could damage our relationship with them. In such circumstances, the regulators could also order corrective action and/or fines against Bolt.

[~accountid:712020:7f47c2af-14e1-4206-a795-ac87cb906276] 

* What you refer to is one aspect of the regulatory issues. As section “[+Split payouts from Service Provider income+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1AZ6R3pQcPhwHNTbSdXytaZeG3T1CvIgO0N50WP1DcK4/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.rkl3hcgdj55a]” in FinReg Playbook further explains, the key issue around making split payments to third parties is that this significantly increases the risk that we may not fit under commercial agent exemption, which in turn would trigger need for payments license. This is why we allow it only in limited cases and on conditions to the setup, as described in the FinReg Playbook. As such, the following comments remain valid:
** Key open issue is whether there are there any feasible alternatives to such setup.
*** E.g. Is there any other way to ensure discounts.
*** E.g. Can payments to aggregator generally be made by fleet, but vis a vis to aggregator Bolt undertakes credit risk by guaranteeing to pay fleet debt (and vis a vis fleet have contractual right to then take this money back from fleet’s earnings).
** If there’s any other feasible alternative, my recommendation is to go for that one, assuming we want to define/implement a long term scalable solution. Any later revamp, especially if we partner with several aggregators costs us resource.
** Debt collection: This assessment should come from Legal Team.

** Encourage the need to rest
** Explain that they can accept rides again when their resting time is over, they can find that in the app
** If driver is confused, explain to them that their work time is calculated within a *rolling* 24 hours (not fixed, e.g. at midnight)

In contrast to, for example, resale Billing Mode, where on the Ride Invoices the BA details will not be present. in this case, Bolt will issue the monthly invoice for the Rides. *Rough Estimation*
From a human resource perspective, I’d estimate around 8 man-days for this project, covering design documentation, requesting resources, implementation, and testing.*Resource Estimation*
The actual resource costs depend, but based on napkin calculations using the conditions we have:

* Spike Duration: 1 hour
* Event Rate: 55k events/sec
* Target Throttling Rate: 20k events/sec
* Excess Events to Buffer: 35k events/sec
* Total Messages to Store in SQS for 1 Hour: 35k * 60 * 60 = 126M messages*SQS Cost Calculation*


Each message requires 3 requests (Put, Receive, Delete):

* Total API requests per spike: 126M * 3 = 378M requests
* SQS Pricing: $0.40 per 1M requests
* Total Cost for 1-hour spike: 378M / 1M * 0.40 = ~$150 per spike*How Many Spikes Do We Have?*
* In the last 2 weeks, we had 4 spikes.
* Most spikes last 10 minutes, not 1 hour.
* A 10-minute spike costs: $150 / 6 = ~$25 per spike
* If we have 10 spikes per month, the cost would be: 10 * 25 = ~$250/month for SQS*Redis Cost Estimation*
* Redis is relatively cheap, assuming a 1GB instance.
* Approximate cost: ~$10/month*Final Cost Summary*
* SQS (No Batching): ~$250/month → ~$3.1K/year
* Redis: ~$10/month → ~$120/year
* Total (No Batching): ~$260/month → ~$3.1K/year
* Total (With Batching): ~$125/month → ~$1.5K/year*Notes:*
* Costs could be reduced ~50% with batching.
* Human effort: ~8 man-days
* Costs scale linearly if spikes increase.

Hello,
There was an issue in our legacy system that affected the calculation of the *start balance* for each billing period. This issue began with the July 2019 [invoice|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/business-invoicing/businessCompanies/edit/3221?tab=invoices&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A50%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D] (ID: 44206), where a refund of *0.83* euros was applied.
As a result, in the August 2019 invoice, the *start balance* was recorded as *3.02* euros instead of the correct *3.85* euros (which was the service fee amount from the previous period). Even though we correctly charged the *3.85* euro service fee(check [balance entries|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/business-invoicing/businessCompanies/edit/3221?tab=balance_entries&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22limit%22%3A50%2C%22business_company_id%22%3A3221%2C%22created_from%22%3A1561928400%2C%22created_to%22%3A1564866000%7D%7D]), the system miscalculated the start balance, likely due to a legacy bug in the system at that time.

This small difference of *0.86* euros (*0.83* euros from the refund + *0.03* euros from rounding) carried forward through each billing period until the company transitioned to a postpaid model in December 2023. In the November 2023 invoice, the service fee was *66.62* euros, but the start balance for December 2023 was *65.76* euros — *0.86* euros short.

In January 2024(company switched to postpaid), this difference was adjusted by *reducing* their invoice amount by *0.86* euros. As a result, they ended up paying *0.86 euros less* than they should have, which is leading to an *overdue balance of 0.86 euro*.

*Summary*
This was not an error on the company’s part—they have always paid the amounts, we've invoiced. However, due to a legacy system issue, we mistakenly invoiced *0.86* euros less than the actual amount. This means the company still owes *0.86* euros, which originated from a miscalculation of start balance in July 2019.

*What to do next?*
Let's add an apology credit of *0.86* euros to clear the overdue balance from the company's account. This way, we can make things right and keep the customer happy.

h2. *Driver GMV* 

In order to understand what gmv we may be hurting with our block actions, I’ve compiled the *average weekly earnings per driver based on their past monthly performance* - their average weekly clean GMV (no fraud markings, no payment issues). 

As we have two types of suspensions here: cases that end up with a permanent stop and cases that end up with temporary limitations. 

With temporary limitations, we have somewhat a better picture as we know they were off the platform for certain amount of time and can correlate their usual earning with what they missed out on. However, this is an oversight on our part: we do not offer a timely solution between driver and rider to inform them in good time about a CCTV camera that a driver wants to use for his own safety. The rider only has the option of canceling the trip after the driver has already arrived and has noticed the CCTV camera and does not agree to it. The product therefore bears some of the responsibility for this misunderstanding.

This case is the extreme exception and cannot be declared a rule. 

This is why the product should be designed so that riders are informed *after being matched with a driver* if a vehicle has CCTV, allowing them to make an informed choice upfront. If riders can see this information in advance and still *choose not to cancel before the arrival*, then cancelling due to CCTV - the cancellation fees would be collected from riders. This ensures transparency, reduces last-minute cancellations, and avoids placing the cost burden on drivers unfairly.

Hello Kertu,

As discussed on Slack,  Lidl LV will Bolt at the end of the promotion period for the remuneration of advertising services.  The remuneration is calculated based on the discounts used by Lidl’s clients. So the contract can be signed with Bolt EE (EE VAT ID).

Dear Damir,

Thank you for your message on 14 February 2025.

As mentioned in our previous message, iOS devices (including the iOS device linked to your Bolt account) enable apps to automatically trigger notifications when the user enters a specific geographic area (including airports). It is not Bolt that is collecting your location information in this context, but instead Apple, and so this does not require the Bolt app to run in the background. Apple stores this location information on their side, and will automatically trigger notifications when a user enters a defined geographic area, without sharing the user’s location with Bolt.

In your case, what this likely means is that Apple collected your location information via your iOS device, including when you were in the airport in Madrid. Since this iOS device is linked to your Bolt account, this automatically triggered a notification to be sent to you regarding Bolt’s services in Madrid. This did not require the Bolt app to be open.

We therefore reiterate that Bolt does not collect your location information when the Bolt app is closed. Bolt only collects your location information in the foreground when the app is open. We hope that this addresses your concerns.

If you have any additional questions, please let us know.

Yours sincerely,

*Bolt*

* {{input}} is not empty → means, the user has typed something
* the user has enough permissions

* Current user → always available, no API calls needed
* GAC responsible admin user → only, if the admin user ID is specified in GAC.

+*BACKGROUND:*+

* As part of a branding project, we want to find 5 people in 7 markets (presumably just riders) who are willing to film a promotional video, who would be awarded Bolt credits as a result.
* Question is whether we can send an invitation to our entire user base via email (i.e., sending an email to hundreds of thousands of users).

+*ANALYSIS*+

* Many of the questions here are not Privacy questions - this is definitely more for Legal.
* In terms of sending the emails:
** *Legal basis*:
*** Arguably legitimate interest would be most appropriate here. Consent is not objectively required here.
*** LIA would be preferable to implement :target: - unlikely that one already exists. Added to [+backlog+|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1lyScH1kZNk1-FeUbmkAdOBDbmbuYkBACcCvwG6EuhF4/edit?gid=0#gid=0].
*** However, in terms of necessity test, it is questionable whether every single email is needed for this purpose - this seems disproportionate ❗ 
** *Transparency*: 
*** Covered by passenger privacy notice (“_To market and advertise Bolt services and those of partners according to your preferences and measure the effectiveness of Bolt’s ads_”) (/) 
**** (NB. Not covered in driver privacy notice, so if we are sending to drivers, we may need to include some disclaimer language)
** *Risks*:
*** Main risk is disproportionality, as processing email addresses on a potentially large scale. Data categories / effects are not otherwise high risk.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Check that this is presumably just riders.
* Advise that we should try and narrow the scope of people we are sending this to. Disproportionate and intrusive to send emails to everyone.
* Flag that GFT should also review, as there are other potentially more pressing concerns.
* If we go ahead with this, add LIA to backlog.

{quote}Dear Jeff,



Thank you for following up to our response dated *5 March 2025*.



This response addresses your request from *5 March 2025* related to the retention period of personal data Bolt keeps for tax, accounting and financial reporting purposes, where you requested a response to the following questions:



# Provide more details on the legal grounds Bolt relies on under GDPR to justify retaining personal data beyond the legally required 7-year period
# What specific types of legal claims or disputes require retaining your personal data for an additional three years and whether there have been past cases where this extended period was necessary
# Information about specific jurisdictions where Bolt operates that require a 10-year retention period





*Answer to Question 1 and 3*



As stated in our previous response dated 5 March 2025 (‘*_Response_*’), GDPR allows controllers, such as Bolt, to keep personal data for as long as this is necessary for the purposes for which the personal data are collected (Art 5(1)(e)). Bolt has a legal obligation to keep the financial data for 7 years in Estonia under the Accounting Act and for up to 10 years in other locations Bolt operates, such as Germany, under the German Tax Code. As mentioned in the Response, Bolt is allowed to keep data longer than it’s required by the local law if this is necessary for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims such as tax audits, potential disputes or claims. In this case Bolt relies on the legitimate interest under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR.



*Answer to Question 2*



Bolt retains accounting source documents, such as invoices for completed orders, to ensure consistent compliance across all jurisdictions Bolt operates in and to address tax audits, potential disputes or claims. 



We would like to clarify that information about past cases where the accounting source documents were necessary for related tax audits, disputes or claims comprises the confidential information of Bolt and is not included in the scope of data subject rights request.



We hope this response clarifies your concerns.



Sincerely,

Bolt{quote}

Here's a run-through of the issues from my perspective. Have a read through and then we can have a call if needed?

* *Our practices on making invoices / receipts available:*
** we will need to comply with all relevant formalities for invoices and receipts (as applicable ) ;
** the people who are best able to say whether any proposals will do with will be *tax / commerce*;
** if *tax / commerce* are happy with the proposals for the market, then I am also happy

* *Provisions in our terms and conditions regarding how invoices are provided:*
** this is a 'legal team only' point - there are no "blockers";
** all we need to do is make sure there is flexibility in how we operate;
** as discussed, we can add some tweaks to ensure that our "notice" provisions do not restrict how we circulate invoices

* *Formal legal notices (generally):*
** This includes things such as:
*** terms and conditions changes;
*** notices regarding 'material action' that Bolt will be taking in accordance with rights reserved its terms;
*** material actions: something significant that somebody will care about / would be very annoyed about if he didn't know about it.
** Anything like that should be sent in a durable medium: email or a letter, in addition to any 'in-app notifications' that we might also send.
** This is because it's inappropriate (and probably unlawful) to expect any user to have to use and open our technology to understand things which may financially affect them.
** The more impactful the change / message, the more it warrants a formal notice.
** Example (silly, but for the sake of illustrating the point):
*** _Bolt: "hey - we've decided to just keep a bunch of money because of [reasons] unless you let us know x, y, z in 7 days."_
*** *7 days pass - user never opens the Bolt app / has notifications off*
*** _User: ".... wtf!!! you never notified me"_ <--- probably right to be justifiably annoyed.
*** However, he would have no grounds for complaint if we also sent an email.

In general, bailiffs have an authority to collect debts, which include deductions from payments owed to a debtor. However, the rules for making deductions from payments depend on the nature of the debtor's income and the related legal framework. 

If the debtor is a service provider (e.g., self-employed person) rather than an employee, the bailiff can still seek to enforce the debt. However, the bailiff's ability to make deductions from payments depends on whether the debtor is receiving regular income, such as payments from clients. There are limitations to how much can be deducted, and the amount deducted must respect certain exemptions set out by law, such as a minimum income threshold that the debtor can keep for their livelihood.

The accounting team or any other team that is responsible for payments / deductions located in Estonia, shall take a look at this as well and, if needed, to reach out to the bailiff directly to clarify if all is in order (the contracts are available in the provided document).

Hi [~accountid:712020:822a759a-daf0-4161-afbf-8b79a2985fba]  and [~accountid:5e343c77a7f27d0e6c6d6698] , my thoughts below:

* *Type 1 refunds: refunds customers are entitled to, such as in cases of total, partial or inadequate performance by Bolt*
** Setting a time limit shorter than the statutory one and enforcing it would be risky. In the EU, such a practice would likely be considered unfair under consumer laws. The EU Unfair Contract Terms Directive (93/13/EEC) lists as an example of unfair terms those “inappropriately excluding or limiting the legal rights of the consumer (…) in the event of total or partial non-performance or inadequate performance by the seller or supplier of any of the contractual obligations”.
** To better map out the risks, a country-specific review would be necessary. However, such a provision could lead to fines from authorities and would likely be deemed null and void in the event of a legal dispute. Statutory limitation periods for refunds indeed vary from jurisdiction to jurisdiction.
** A possible risk-mitigation could be to establish a soft guideline for customers to contact CS. That seems to be the approach in Uber France T&Cs shared by [~accountid:712020:822a759a-daf0-4161-afbf-8b79a2985fba], where it’s said customers should contact CS within 30 days without apparently it being a hard deadline. However, if Bolt were to enforce this limitation and deny refunds solely based on its expiration, this would be at the same level of risk as above. Setting longer time limits (e.g., 6 months) could help reduce customer complaints, though it would not materially decrease legal exposure - more of a practical risk mitigation measure.
* *Type 2 refunds: compensational refunds, AKA goodwill payments or discretionary compensations*
** It should be fine to impose a time limit for these payments from a legal standpoint. However, how would this work in practice? From my understanding, CS uses these payments to manage customer frustration with a poor experience with Bolt. They are granted at Bolt’s discretion, usually only when customers complain to CS. 
** If a customer were to contact CS after the established timeframe, how would CS handle the situation? Would they acknowledge the poor experience but deny compensation due to a missed deadline? Wouldn’t this undermine the very purpose of such compensations?

Let me know if you would like to chat about the above.

Thanks and best,

Thiago

Hi [~accountid:712020:c190ab8b-4add-4eb3-bd6e-ab39d6c1cd0c],

Here are the key legal concerns to consider in Spain regarding the proposed Family Account Terms:

h3. *1. Consumer Protection*

* *Liability of the Family Account Owner & Termination Due to Violations by Family Members:*
** Spanish consumer protection laws (Royal Legislative Decree 1/2007 of 16 November 2007) require clear and transparent information regarding the legal terms of contracts with users. Additionally, Article 82 of the aforementioned law establishes that clauses imposing disproportionate obligations or guarantees on the consumer shall be considered abusive and, therefore, null and void.
** In this context, 
*** The clause stating that the Family Account Owner accepts full responsibility for all activities conducted through the Family Account, including those of family members, could be viewed as overly broad. This may raise concerns about proportionality and enforceability. It would be +advisable to revise this language to provide more precise details regarding the scope of the Family Account Owner's responsibility, for instance, by adding exceptions to their liability+ (such as fraud, unauthorized use, or technical errors attributable to Bolt).
*** The termination of a Family Account due to violations committed by any account member could potentially be seen as disproportionate. In my opinion, +the Family Account Owner should not automatically lose access if another member commits a violation+, unless they were directly involved or failed to take reasonable steps to prevent the misuse or violation. Furthermore, to ensure fairness, it may be advisable to +implement an internal appeals mechanism in order to challenge termination decisions made by Bolt based on violations committed by any Family Account member+.
* *Age Requirement (18+) & Minors*:
** Spanish law (Código Civil, Article 315) establishes 18 as the legal age of adulthood, granting individuals full capacity to perform all civil acts. 
** However, minors are subject to certain restrictions when entering into contracts. Under the Spanish Civil Code, minors generally cannot enter into contracts without the explicit consent of their legal guardian, except for contracts related to routine daily activities. In light of this, I +recommend that the Family Account Owner can only add minors to the Family Account if they are the parents or legal guardians of the minor+, and should confirm this when doing so.
** Please find my +proposal+ for the terms below:

*_Terms for the Family Account Owner_*

_When adding members to your Family Account, you confirm that:_

* _They are either 18 years old or older, or_
* _If they are a minor, you: i) Are their parent or legal guardian, and ii) Acknowledge and understand that Bolt has no obligation to consult or seek consent from any other parent or guardian._

_—>_ Nb: *Clause 1.6* of the *ES Passenger T&Cs* specifies:*:*
 _"You must be at least 18 years old to access the Bolt application, including accepting these General Terms and Conditions. Additionally, you must ensure that any individuals using transportation services through the Bolt application on your behalf are also at least 18 years old. The driver has the right to deny service to the passenger or any other person using the services on behalf of the passenger who cannot prove they are at least 18 years old."_

+For minors added to a Family Account to be subject to our T&Cs, we would need to update this clause accordingly.+

 

h3. *2. Privacy and Data Protection*

* *Sharing of Personal Data Among Family Members*:
** The provision stating that "Profile visibility exists between all Family Account members" *might raise GDPR concerns*. +This should be discussed with the Privacy team+, as under Spanish Data Protection Law (LOPDGDD) and the GDPR (Regulation EU 2016/679), it +may be necessary to obtain explicit, informed consent before sharing personal data between members+.
** To address this, it may be advisable to introduce a privacy settings feature for Family Account members, allowing them to control the visibility of their data. Only the data strictly necessary for the functionality of the service should be shared. However, please consult with the privacy team for confirmation and further guidance.

h3. *3. Governing Law & Jurisdiction*

* In accordance with EU consumer protection regulations, consider clarifying that: 
** The Terms shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of the user’s country of residence. 
** The jurisdiction for any legal disputes shall be the user’s country of residence.

Hi [~accountid:712020:822a759a-daf0-4161-afbf-8b79a2985fba], I would like to share my feedback regarding the privacy aspects outlined in the Terms and Conditions (T&Cs).

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
In summary:

I cannot recommend proceeding with the provider in its current form. I strongly suggest concluding a custom DPA based on our draft before moving forward, as several critical data protection clauses are missing, including provisions for data deletion.

If the platform is used minimally and does not involve sensitive personal data, the risks of proceeding as is would be low. Nonetheless, the overall compliance of Willo is inadequate and requires significant improvement.
{panel}

*Details:*

The relevant sections include:
# Section 11 on data protection; and
# A Data Processing Addendum (DPA) attached as Annex 1.
Upon review, I believe that the default privacy clauses provided by Willo do not meet the necessary standards for data protection and compliance with the GDPR. My primary concerns are as follows:
# *Data Subject Rights Assistance*
# *Data Breach Notification*
# *Data Deletion or Return upon Termination*
# *Data Protection Audit Rights for Bolt*
# *International Data Transfers* - While not explicitly mentioned, this is a minor risk considering the organization is UK-based. However, it could pose a problem in the future if EU authorities reconsider the UK as a safe data transfer destination and require additional safeguards.
Although the T&Cs state that the Supplier will process personal data in compliance with applicable data protection laws, they lack the necessary details on the aforementioned points, which are explicitly required under the GDPR. Therefore, we could already be considered in breach if we agree to the T&Cs along with the attached incomplete DPA.
----
Furthermore, the DPA within the T&Cs does not align with our internal DPA standards, particularly concerning clauses mandated by law. Specifically:
# *Security Measures* - Willo fails to specify the information security measures it will implement in the document. Clause 11.4 of the T&Cs merely states that the Supplier must implement "appropriate technical and organisational measures." While its [Security and Data Whitepaper|https://cvsd004.na1.hs-sales-engage.com/Ctc/I6+23284/cVSD004/JlY2-6qcW95jsWP6lZ3mdW1NYQL92BqbgWW8cmKhR3mL29RN6ZBY0f8PSG5W7nFF6S1SN0BPN6KrTy0kTfSsW7TWRt86L5NJSN5YFhd6S1SR8N8v_FThT3RTRW7Qs3-S1wBKLsN8gKTqDkQDDWW9353T48HmzMpW6q-RyY2mH-xqW6NpTtZ3zK-R8W8XRVkL1Wk_pyW7byJ8D84T0dQW8zTD934yVnf5N8cTtDpttXcrW15KDG45N-fkXW5nJmvv6MqG-7W5mTJ8_6GXz_MW30955h56KqY2VbDqd34F8sfcW4w12B12-W8X7VFG9rd3hqZV9N4cFTst7Lqd_W6dxcZq72Fd7JW5Npdqk8xvDC5W4R8G5898_GyTVTM1446BGPtSW6rN4795TbDk7f6G6qXl04] appears robust, the DPA in the T&Cs should ideally reference specific security measures. Typically, Bolt requires suppliers to accept its [https://bolt.eu/en/security/|https://bolt.eu/en/security/|smart-link] or for Bolt to review the list of custom measures provided by the supplier.
# *Engagement of Sub-Processors* - Generally, Bolt requires a minimum of 30 days' specific prior authorisation for sub-processors. # A Data Processing Addendum (DPA) attached as Annex 1.
Upon review, I believe that the default privacy clauses provided by Willo do not meet the necessary standards for data protection and compliance with the GDPR. My primary concerns are as follows:
# *Data Subject Rights Assistance*
# *Data Breach Notification*
# *Data Deletion or Return upon Termination*
# *Data Protection Audit Rights for Bolt*
# *International Data Transfers* - While not explicitly mentioned, this is a minor risk considering the organization is UK-based. However, it could pose a problem in the future if EU authorities reconsider the UK as a safe data transfer destination and require additional safeguards.
Although the T&Cs state that the Supplier will process personal data in compliance with applicable data protection laws, they lack the necessary details on the aforementioned points, which are explicitly required under the GDPR. Therefore, we could already be considered in breach if we agree to the T&Cs along with the attached incomplete DPA.
----
Furthermore, the DPA within the T&Cs does not align with our internal DPA standards, particularly concerning clauses mandated by law. Specifically:
# *Security Measures* - Willo fails to specify the information security measures it will implement in the document. Clause 11.4 of the T&Cs merely states that the Supplier must implement "appropriate technical and organisational measures." While its [Security and Data Whitepaper|https://cvsd004.na1.hs-sales-engage.com/Ctc/I6+23284/cVSD004/JlY2-6qcW95jsWP6lZ3mdW1NYQL92BqbgWW8cmKhR3mL29RN6ZBY0f8PSG5W7nFF6S1SN0BPN6KrTy0kTfSsW7TWRt86L5NJSN5YFhd6S1SR8N8v_FThT3RTRW7Qs3-S1wBKLsN8gKTqDkQDDWW9353T48HmzMpW6q-RyY2mH-xqW6NpTtZ3zK-R8W8XRVkL1Wk_pyW7byJ8D84T0dQW8zTD934yVnf5N8cTtDpttXcrW15KDG45N-fkXW5nJmvv6MqG-7W5mTJ8_6GXz_MW30955h56KqY2VbDqd34F8sfcW4w12B12-W8X7VFG9rd3hqZV9N4cFTst7Lqd_W6dxcZq72Fd7JW5Npdqk8xvDC5W4R8G5898_GyTVTM1446BGPtSW6rN4795TbDk7f6G6qXl04] appears robust, the DPA in the T&Cs should ideally reference specific security measures. Typically, Bolt requires suppliers to accept its [https://bolt.eu/en/security/|https://bolt.eu/en/security/|smart-link] or for Bolt to review the list of custom measures provided by the supplier.
# *Engagement of Sub-Processors* - Generally, Bolt requires a minimum of 30 days' specific prior authorisation for sub-processors. However, in this case, Willo provides general authorisation and just 14 days' notice. While we can generally accept “general authorisation”, we require at least 20 days notification to adequately assess a new sub-processor and evaluate associated risks.

Onboarding Status



Some markets require drivers to come to hub
Others have action that needs to be taken before lead can be accepted

Compliance team has developed onboarding status that is tied to comms

Basic flow to support:

# Driver* submits application

# Lead acceptance commences -> do all checks, tasks, conflict-resolution, but don't actually create anything (ie: driver, car, etc. -- no actions)

# Pause lead acceptance

# Set status to 'Onboarding' (compliance team has implemented this)

# UI: On driver's registration page, create a button** to continue auto-acceptance

# Driver completes action (ie: comes in to the hub)

# Ops ensure that the action is completed and do an audit of all documents, and then press button created in step 5

# Lead-acceptance is completed*** -> ie: perform all actions



* Driver is in a market that has an onboarding step that takes a long time (ie: come to the hub, mail in signage, or complete some other action on their own, etc.)

** Do not create button if lead acceptance fails -> just fail automatic acceptance, ops will take care of the rest

*** Skip audit in these cases -- assumption is that the audit will be done together with ensuring that the driver has completed the requested action

Thanks for raising a ticket with the legal team. I have now looked into your query.

My interpretation of the term “toll” in the UK is usually a reference to a fee or a charge that has to be paid for using certain roads, bridges or tunnels (for example, the Dartford Crossing toll fee). Whereas, fines and penalties are usually a fee charged for breaking the law or failing to comply with certain regulations (for example, a speeding fine or parking ticket - penalty charge notice).

While a failure to pay a toll can lead to a fine, the term "toll" itself doesn't imply a fine, so I don’t see any issues with the current wording.

Given this, I’m comfortable with updating the price breakdown as suggested, as you mentioned it adds clarity for both drivers and passengers, and I don’t see any legal risks. h2. 🐝 Handling callback requests in Beehive

*Callback Request Handling*

The callback request feature allows users to request a call from Support on their registered phone number. When handling these requests, please follow these steps:

# *User verification:* Following the established verification guidelines outlined in [🌍 User verification guidelines|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/8671806622098?country=global&language=en] all callback requests come from verified channels
# *Review the request:*
#* Click "Assign to me" to pick up the request
#* Carefully read the user's message to understand their issue.
#* Check for any additional messages sent after the callback request.
# *Prepare for the call:*
#* If the user sent a message after the callback request, *call them first*. (You may follow up with a message after the call if needed.)
#* If the user is hard of hearing (as indicated in their message), respond with an in-app message instead of calling.
#* Open the user profile and review their current order to gain context.
# *Initiate the call:*
#* Click the "Call" button in Beehive.
#* Allow the phone to ring until it disconnects (usually 45 seconds).
# *The user doesn’t answer:*
#* If the user doesn't answer after the first attempt, close the Wrap-up modal by clicking "X" and try calling again.
#* Make the second call attempt with a *2-minute* interval between each attempt.
#* *If the user still doesn't answer:*
#** After two unsuccessful attempts, click the "Close" button and select "Customer not answering."
#** Complete the form and click "Close Request." The user will receive an automated message, and the ticket will automatically close after 5 days. 
# *The user answers:*

* Introduce yourself and explain that you are following up on their callback request
* Ask them to describe their issue and resolve it following the relevant internal process
** If the user wishes to discuss or requests to change *personal data*, inform them that we can only resolve their issue via an in-app message
* After the callback has been performed, leave an internal note with any relevant information structured like this:
** Issue/request: _e.g Driver reported an incorrect fare on their last order._
** Steps taken: _e.g, Verified the fare details, identified a discrepancy, and adjusted the fare accordingly._
** Outcome: _e.g Fare corrected, driver reimbursed._
** Next step: _e.g, Not required_

*Additional information for* 🥡 *Bolt Food callbacks*

* Call the user only once

*Provider callbacks*

* Always respond to the callback by calling the Provider
* If the provider doesn’t reply: + If there is a message included with the callback, provide the solution based on the message. End the message by saying that if they still need a call, they should let us know.
** If there is no message or the issue isn’t clear from the message, write to the provider asking them for more information. Set the ticket to Pending.

*Courier callbacks*

* If either of the conditions is met, call the courier:
** The order has not been delivered
** You are within the 5 min SLO
* If neither of the conditions are met, follow the same process for instances when the provider doesn’t reply.

*Additional information for 🚙 Bolt Drive callbacks*

* When you've ended the call, complete the Call Wrap-up and click _Submit_
* After making the call, remove the issue tag "_No issue found in the list_" and replace it with the correct issue tag. 
* *Note:* Currently, the page is not updated automatically. You need to refresh the page after you finish the call wrap-up in order to see the changes made to the case.

h2. 🐝 Handling callback requests in Beehive

*Callback Request Handling*

The callback request feature allows users to request a call from Support on their registered phone number. When handling these requests, please follow these steps:

# *User verification:* Following the established verification guidelines outlined in [🌍 User verification guidelines|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/8671806622098?country=global&language=en] all callback requests come from verified channels
# *Review the request:*
#* Click "Assign to me" to pick up the request
#* Carefully read the user's message to understand their issue.
#* Check for any additional messages sent after the callback request.
# *Prepare for the call:*
#* If the user sent a message after the callback request, *call them first*. (You may follow up with a message after the call if needed.)
#* If the user is hard of hearing (as indicated in their message), respond with an in-app message instead of calling.
#* Open the user profile and review their current order to gain context.
#* *🥡 Bolt Food - Provider:* Always call the provider upon request
#** If the provider doesn’t reply: 
#*** If there is a message included with the callback, provide the solution based on the message. End the message by saying that if they still need a call, they should let us know.
#*** If there is no message or the issue isn’t clear from the message, write to the provider asking them for more information. Set the ticket to Pending.
#* *🥡 Bolt Food - Courier:* Call the courier if the following conditions are met
#** The order has not been delivered
#** You are within the 5 min SLO
#** If neither of the conditions are met, follow the same process for instances when the *Provider* doesn’t reply.
# *Initiate the call:*
#* Click the "Call" button in Beehive.
#* Allow the phone to ring until it disconnects (usually 45 seconds).
#* *🥡 Bolt Food:* Call the user only once
# *The user doesn’t answer:*
#* If the user doesn't answer after the first attempt, close the Wrap-up modal by clicking "X"
#* Make the second call attempt with a *2-minute* interval between each attempt.
#* *If the user still doesn't answer:*
#** After two unsuccessful attempts, click the "Close" button and select "Customer not answering."
#** Complete the form and click "Close Request." The user will receive an automated message, and the ticket will automatically close after 5 days.
# *The user answers:*

* Introduce yourself and explain that you are following up on their callback request
* Ask them to describe their issue and resolve it following the relevant internal process
** If the user wishes to discuss or requests to change *personal data*, inform them that we can only resolve their issue via an in-app message
* When you've ended the call, complete the Call Wrap-up and click _Submit_
* After the callback has been performed, leave an internal note with any relevant information structured like this:
** Issue/request: _e.g Driver reported an incorrect fare on their last order._
** Steps taken: _e.g, Verified the fare details, identified a discrepancy, and adjusted the fare accordingly._
** Outcome: _e.g Fare corrected, driver reimbursed._
** Next step: _e.g, Not required_
* *🚙 Bolt Drive:* After making the call, remove the issue tag "_No issue found in the list_" and replace it with the correct issue tag.
** *Note:* Currently, the page is not updated automatically. You need to refresh the page after you finish the call wrap-up in order to see the changes made to the case.

Hi team, 

The user is reporting a authorization double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer. 
You can ask the customer to reach out to their bank in order to confirm the authorized funds have been released. Their bank can locate the funds with the authorization date and amount. 


Please let me know if you have any other questions.

Cheers,
Marten

*Feedback from markets*

One of the main concerns from LOPS related to brake actuators is the brake actuator pin from seizing to the housing, immobilizing the brake. To tackle that issue, LOPS disassembles the pin, cleans the surfaces and greases them, then reassembles. While the cleaning process is OK, the brake actuator still seizes soon.

Most likely one of the reasons we get this seizing is galvanic corrosion - the pin is steel and the housing is aluminum, which creates the conditions for galvanic corrosion. There is no bushing for the steel pin either and there is also friction between the pin and the housing from using the brake. Whatever seal we use under the pin is also not too helpful in keeping water and salt away, so together with the galvanic corrosion between steel and aluminum and friction between metal surfaces, we also have salt there as the accelerator for corrosion.

Perhaps a way to improve the seizing situation would be to have a spacer/bushing between the aluminum housing and steel pin - maybe IGUS plastics/composites or copper/brass/bronze? Something which would not naturally corrode that bad and would not cause galvanic corrosion.

The time estimated for tax support to this project is meant to provide advice and support to ensure the accurate VAT treatment of long-term hire of vehicles.

In summary:

* Short-term hire of vehicles (less than 30 days in a row) is subject to VAT where the vehicle is put at the customer’s disposal, either if the customer is a private individual or a business customer.
* Long-term hire of vehicles (30+ days) is subject to VAT:
** Where the service provider is established for VAT purposes if the customer is a private individual (B2C)
** Where the customer is established for VAT purposes if the customer is a business (B2B).
* The VAT treatment of long-term hire of vehicles may be more complex if the customer is a Bolt Business customer.

This would apply in the scenario where there's no response from the reported party after 24 or 48 hours, when you close the tool, it will prompt you to apply a Customer Safety Support Block. This block remains until the reported party provides feedback.

When the reported party eventually comes back, the case will be addressed based on the facts gathered and a different consequential action may be taken. Eg warning, education, 28-day block etc. This should be updated in the tool and also reflected in the closing notes since the Customer Safety Support block would be lifted from the reported party’s account.

In this ticket; [+https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/500642208+|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/500642208] , the rider responded after the tool was closed and a block was placed on their account. However, after gathering further information, the rider was educated and the block was lifted. Given that this is not stated in KB, the agent failed to amend the tool with the information gathered and the consequential action taken. Also, the closing notes were not updated on the ticket and the admin order page.  In this instance, the information in the tool and the closing notes would be inconsistent with the new action taken.

The purpose of creating this SD is to request an addition to KB which categorically states the next steps to take when a user responds after the tool is closed *without a response from the reported party*. 

Eg. When the reporting party responds after the tool is closed and a CSS block is placed on their account:

* Ask them to share their account of the event

* Update the tool with the information gathered and take the relevant action based on your outcome (consequential blocks as suggested by the tool or deviant actions)

* Update the closing notes to reflect the actions taken. The reasoning here is that it's not all the time a penalty would be issued. Hence, its factored into this steps.

It would be appropriate to include in KB the specific format to use when updating the closing notes in this regard.

+*BACKGROUND*+

** “_I don’t think there will be any personal data processed on our side other than the contact data of persons responsible for the implementation of the agreement (name and surname, phone number, email address)_.”
* Privacy has been asked to review data protection provisions (para 18).
** 1. _The landlord_ [PKP] _declares that he is the data controller within the meaning of … the GDPR, with regard to the personal data of the Landlord who is a natural person, natural persons representing the Landlord and natural persons indicated by this entity as contact persons and other persons responsible for the performance of this Agreement (if indicated)._
** _2. Contact details of the data protection officer of the landlord: iod@pkp.pl,_ [_www.pkp.pl/RODO_|http://www.pkp.pl/RODO]_, Al. Jerozolimskie 142A, 02-305 Warsaw_
** _3. The landlord informs that the legal basis for the processing of personal data is:_
_a. Article 6(1)(b) of the GDPR – fulfilment of contractual requirements, i.e. the need to have data at one's disposal for the performance of the concluded Contract1,_
_b. Article 6(1)(c) of the GDPR – fulfilment of statutory requirements, i.e. the need for the Landlord to fulfil legal obligations arising from the law,_
_c. Article 6(1)(f) of the GDPR – the need to fulfil the Lessor's legitimate interests related to ensuring the proper implementation of the Agreement, including the possible establishment, investigation or defence against claims related to the concluded Agreement._
** _4. The personal data referred to in point 1 will not be transferred to third parties, however, in accordance with applicable law, the Landlord may transfer the data to entities processing it on behalf of the Landlord, e.g. on the basis of personal data processing agreements with IT service providers, auditors, advisors, and on the basis of applicable law to entities authorised to obtain data, e.g. courts or law enforcement agencies - only when they request personal data and indicate the legal basis for their request._
** _5. The personal data of the persons specified in point 1 will not be transferred to a third country or an international organisation within the meaning of the GDPR._
** _6. The personal data of the persons referred to in point 1 will be processed for a period of 10 years from the end of the calendar year in which this Agreement is performed, unless a longer period of processing is necessary, e.g. due to archiving obligations, the pursuit of claims or other requirements of generally applicable law._
** _7. The persons referred to in point 1 have the right to request the data controller to access their personal data, rectify it, delete or limit the processing of the data or object to its processing, as well as the right to data portability. These rights will be exercised by the Landlord within the limits of applicable law._
** _8. The persons referred to in point 1 have the right to lodge a complaint with the supervisory authority, i.e. the President of the Office for Personal Data Protection, in connection with the processing of their personal data._
** _9. The provision of personal data referred to in point 1 is required to conclude the Agreement. If the aforementioned natural person requests the deletion or limitation of the processing of personal data, the Lessee is obliged to immediately indicate another person to take their place._
** _10. Based on the personal data of the persons referred to in point 1, the Lessor will not make automated decisions, including decisions resulting from profiling within the meaning of the GDPR._
** _11. If the Lessee provides the Lessor with personal data of persons associated with the Lessee, in particular employees, authorised representatives, board members, partners, co-workers, contractors, suppliers, and other persons, the Lessee is obliged to inform these persons on behalf of the Lessor:_
_a. about the scope of personal data concerning these persons, as provided to the Landlord,_
_b. that the Landlord is the controller of their personal data and that they process their personal data in accordance with the rules set out above,_
_c. that the Tenant is the source from which the Landlord obtained their data,_
_d. about the content of this paragraph._

+*ANALYSIS*+

* Provided that the only data being shared is the name and contact details of the signatories, then this is very low risk from a Privacy POV. No obvious blockers.
** Based on the facts, nothing to obviously suggest that Article 28 provisions would be needed.
** Provided it all takes place in Poland, no international data transfers.
** Arguably no need for a data processing Annex. The categories of data are clear, as are legal bases, retention, DPO contact details etc.
** Arguably no need for personal data breach language here. Signatories will know that their personal data is being shared here, and the data is low risk,so very unlikely to go after Bolt.
* Main risk here is that {color:#ff5630}agreement does not contain nor any indemnity{color}. We ordinarily push for these in our standard agreement. However, arguably little point pushing for them here.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Ask stakeholders:

This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer.

Explanation:

* {{ColorReferenceSpan}} requires a view to resolve the color and does it in {{onAttachToView}}
* Spans are parsed on the domain layer (e.g on {{EarnMoreMapper}}) outside of any view.
* The resolved string with span is renderered to {{AppCompatTextView}} which also doesn’t call {{onAttachToView}}, as it is a component from Android and it doesn’t know about our specific spans.
* As a result, colors from spans are never applied. That happens only in the places where {{AppCompatTextView}} is used. Our own {{DesignHtmlTextView}} and {{BoltTextView}} explicitly call {{onAttachToView}} for our spans in {{setText}}.

Solution:

* Agreed with Driver team that they will migrate all {{AppCompatTextView}} to {{TextView}}/{{BoltTextView}} during this week.
* Using {{TextView}} is a valid solution, as Driver’s custom layout inflater instantiates {{DesignHtmlTextView}} for it.
* {{BoltTextView}} is considered to be the best solution for future, but not all styles from Driver UI kit can be easily converted to the ones from the design system. 
* For easier migration, Platform can suggest the inspection in IDE plugin: [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/MP-2330|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/MP-2330|smart-link]

* Query for the final result

{noformat}WITH data_prep AS (
    SELECT
        scc.support_case_id,
        scc.user_id,
        scc.comment,
        bbc.name,
        bbc.last_order,
       DATE_TRUNC('month', scc.created_hour) AS month
    FROM pii.support_case_comments_v2 scc
    LEFT JOIN ng_public.etl_business_business_company bbc
        ON bbc.id = scc.user_id 
    WHERE 
        (lower(scc.comment) like('%service fee%') 
        	or lower(scc.comment) like '%taxas de serviço%'
        	or lower(scc.comment) like '%taxa de serviciu%'
        	or lower(scc.comment) like '%opłaty serwisowej%'
        	or lower(scc.comment) like '%paslaugos mokestį%'
        	or lower(scc.comment) like '%tarifa de servicio%'
        	or lower(scc.comment) like '%poplatku za služby%'
        	or lower(scc.comment) like '%მომსახურების საფასურის%'
        	or lower(scc.comment) like '%teenustasu%'
        	or lower(scc.comment) like '%servicegebühr%'
        	or lower(scc.comment) like '%pakalpojuma maksu%'
        	or lower(scc.comment) like '%xidmət haqqı%')
        AND scc.created_hour > DATE('2024-03-01')
        AND scc.user_type = 'business_company'
)




SELECT 
	month,
    COUNT(DISTINCT support_case_id) AS count_support_cases,
    COUNT(DISTINCT CASE 
        WHEN last_order < DATE_ADD('day', -90, CURRENT_DATE) THEN user_id
    END) AS churned_companies,
    COUNT(DISTINCT CASE
        WHEN last_order >= DATE_ADD('day', -90, CURRENT_DATE) THEN user_id
    END) AS active_companies,
    COUNT(DISTINCT CASE
        WHEN last_order IS NULL THEN user_id 
    END) AS null_last_order_companies
FROM data_prep
group by 1
order by month asc{noformat}
