{noformat}import requests
import openai
import json
from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
from urllib3.util.retry import Retry

# Confluence API credentials
CONFLUENCE_BASE_URL = "https://your-confluence-instance.atlassian.net/wiki"
USERNAME = "your-email@example.com"
API_TOKEN = "your-api-token"
SPACE_KEY = "your-space-key"
PAGE_TITLE = "TiKV Alerts Documentation"

# OpenAI API key
OPENAI_API_KEY = "your-openai-api-key"

def fetch_alerting_rules_from_prometheus(cluster_name) -> list:
    """Fetches alerting rules from Prometheus for a given cluster."""
    url = f"http://{cluster_name}-monitor.sqldb:9090/api/v1/rules"
    alert_names = []

    retry_strategy = Retry(
        total=5,
        backoff_factor=15,
        status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504],
        allowed_methods=["HEAD", "GET", "OPTIONS"],
    )
    adapter = HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retry_strategy)
    http = requests.Session()
    http.mount("http://", adapter)
    http.mount("https://", adapter)

    try:
        response = http.get(url, timeout=10)
        response.raise_for_status()
        data = response.json()

        rules_groups = data.get("data", {}).get("groups", [])
        for group in rules_groups:
            for rule in group.get("rules", []):
                alert_names.append(rule["name"])
                print(f"✅ Alert fetched: {rule['name']}")
        return alert_names

    except (requests.exceptions.RequestException, json.JSONDecodeError) as e:
        print(f"❌ Failed to fetch alerts for {cluster_name}. Error: {e}")
        return []

def generate_alert_info(alert_name):
    """Uses OpenAI to generate descriptions and actions for a given alert."""
    prompt = f"Provide a short description and recommended resolution steps for the TiKV alert '{alert_name}'."
    response = openai.ChatCompletion.create(
        model="gpt-4",
        messages=[{"role": "system", "content": "You are an expert on TiKV and distributed databases."},
                  {"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        api_key=OPENAI_API_KEY,
    )
    return response["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]

def generate_confluence_markup(alerts):
    """Formats the fetched alerts into Confluence wiki markup."""
    content = "h1. TiKV Alerts Documentation\n\n"
    for alert in alerts:
        ai_response = generate_alert_info(alert)
        content += f"h2. {alert}\n{ai_response}\n\n"
    return content

def get_confluence_page():
    """Fetches the page ID and version if the page exists."""
    url = f"{CONFLUENCE_BASE_URL}/rest/api/content"
    params = {
        "title": PAGE_TITLE,
        "spaceKey": SPACE_KEY,
        "expand": "version"
    }
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Basic {requests.auth._basic_auth_str(USERNAME, API_TOKEN)}",
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
    }
    
    response = requests.get(url, params=params, headers=headers)
    if response.status_code == 200:
        results = response.json().get("results", [])
        if results:
            page_id = results[0]["id"]
            version_number = results[0]["version"]["number"]
            return page_id, version_number
    return None, None

def update_confluence_page(page_id, version, content):
    """Updates an existing Confluence page."""
    url = f"{CONFLUENCE_BASE_URL}/rest/api/content/{page_id}"
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Basic {requests.auth._basic_auth_str(USERNAME, API_TOKEN)}",
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
    }
    payload = {
        "id": page_id,
        "type": "page",
        "title": PAGE_TITLE,
        "space": {"key": SPACE_KEY},
        "body": {
            "storage": {
                "value": content,
                "representation": "wiki",
            }
        },
        "version": {
            "number": version + 1
        }
    }
    response = requests.put(url, json=payload, headers=headers)
    if response.status_code in [200, 201]:
        print(f"✅ Page '{PAGE_TITLE}' updated successfully!")
    else:
        print(f"❌ Failed to update page: {response.text}")

def post_to_confluence(content):
    """Creates a new page if not found, otherwise updates the existing one."""
    page_id, version = get_confluence_page()
    
    if page_id:
        print(f"🔄 Page exists. Updating version {version + 1}...")
        update_confluence_page(page_id, version, content)
    else:
        print("🆕 Page not found. Creating a new one...")
        url = f"{CONFLUENCE_BASE_URL}/rest/api/content"
        headers = {
            "Authorization": f"Basic {requests.auth._basic_auth_str(USERNAME, API_TOKEN)}",
            "Content-Type": "application/json",
        }
        payload = {
            "type": "page",
            "title": PAGE_TITLE,
            "space": {"key": SPACE_KEY},
            "body": {
                "storage": {
                    "value": content,
                    "representation": "wiki",
                }
            }
        }
        response = requests.post(url, json=payload, headers=headers)
        if response.status_code in [200, 201]:
            print(f"✅ Page '{PAGE_TITLE}' created successfully!")
        else:
            print(f"❌ Failed to create page: {response.text}")

# Run the process
cluster_name = "your-cluster-name"  # Change this to your actual cluster
alerts = fetch_alerting_rules_from_prometheus(cluster_name)
if alerts:
    confluence_content = generate_confluence_markup(alerts)
    post_to_confluence(confluence_content)
else:
    print("⚠️ No alerts found, skipping Confluence update.")

Hi [~accountid:712020:edb1b22f-4000-4146-9838-14ad9ca1837f] . The BA in question operates under the Intermediate BA Model. The easiest way to understand intermediate model is to think of Bolt as the tool/platform between the driver & rider. The transactions are done between the two & Bolt charges commission for using the platform. 
In this case, all of the invoices for Rides that BA took are issued directly to the BA Details, and hence there’s no need to issue additional invoice for Rides. In order to keep the BA informed, we also monthly statement, which you refer to → it’s an informative summary of the Rides over the previous month.
Worth noting, that in addition to the Monthly Statement, Bolt issues an invoice for the Service Fee, which the BA needs to pay for using the platform.

As of now.
We'll remove the relevant clause from the templates in [Confluence|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/3482320952/Templates.+Business+account] and Spotdraft asap but expect to finalize by end of March.*What do be mindful of with new customers?*
Make sure the accurate limit is reflected for each account in the Company Dashboard.
By default we shouldn't mutually be agreeing on the limit but rather we assign each company a spending limit per their profile.*What do be mindful of with existing customers?*

* Any changes to an existing limit should be well communicated to the customer (ideally in advance and ideally via Dashboard - if available). Especially when increasing the limit based on Bolt's initiative.
* No need to amend the currently signed special terms just for this reason but do remove this clause when an opportunity arises (i.e. smth else triggers the need for amendment in the agreement). However please be mindful that until the clause remains in the agreement it should be kept strictly aligned with the limit shown to the customer in the Dashboard.

*What if a customer itself wants to see this reflected in the agreement?*
Please check out the FAQ in [Business Legal Confluence|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/2923692552/FAQ.+Business+account.+Legal] (under Fees, Payments & Refunds).Any questions - please share in the thread

*Analyzing modelling period change*

Checking whether period per se could make substantial difference (this is main Avishek’s concern). 

For this, I did the following:

* run the same model as were run in Q3 (from the Q3 notebooks folder, [here|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/editor/notebooks/1666917710951523?o=3829506390716583#command/1666917710951524])
* only change the “post” period (additional Q4 data)
* change both “pre” and “post” parts (so that the period is similar to what we have in our actual models for Q4)

Note that 

* priors were not changed at all.
* results were compared to the mean of Q3’s vmax, not the upper bound

Results are collected [here|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1cL6Ur8uJh5oA-DFlrSGYpGsNPc18yik81vORRcSj6Pw/edit?pli=1&gid=2134207199#gid=2134207199] in analyzing_big_drops in columns F, I, K.

* One can see that in France, Germany and Sweden, changing the period does not lead to significant changes in resulting vmax's. 
** The changes for these markets will be analyzed in further comments
* In UK and Poland some (not all) channels changed their coefficients



*Analyzing changes in countries where period per se changed the coefficients.*

Analysis requires that we understand, at which exactly date the coefficient changes. 

We are OK with the situation, where:

* the channel changes after some intervention has happened (i.e. we’ve changed the cost, the model changes the coefficient based on observed results)
* the change happens gradually (not just drops during one week). This would be a sign of model unrobustness.



So for UK and Poland we trained the models that would incrementally add one week from Q3 to Q4 (priors are same) to check the dynamics of the change:

* This was done in [[Automating Periods]|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/editor/notebooks/2934471359380040?o=3829506390716583#command/2934471359380041] folder, results were collected in {{dev_martech_spark.martech_6423_vmax_dynamic}} and analysed in [this|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/editor/notebooks/2934471359373645?o=3829506390716583#command/8478685154296235] notebook.
* The findings are:
** Changes do not happen immediately (over the course of 3-4 weeks)
** Changes happen only when costs are changed (i.e. models obtain additional signal)
** Coefficients are stable before and after the ad change (this confirms that the models are generally robust)

*Checking if the rest of the effect is related to priors.*

There’re are now only two changes that we do Q over Q to the models - changing the period and the priors.

In the previous comment we have shown that additional data only has the impact on coefficients when new data brings new signal (and this is what we want from the model).

Now, it means that the rest of the changes in coefficients should come from changes in priors.  Below we give more details on how it worked out for some markets.

*Stockholm*

* Original Q3 model had very informed priors for iOS keeping the coefficients quite high, like {{{'vmax': {'mu':282, 'sigma':10}}}} (see [here|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/editor/notebooks/2934471359379093?o=3829506390716583#command/2934471359379117])
* Q4 models set the priors to be less informed (with {{sigma=66}} almost for all channels) - see [this|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1cL6Ur8uJh5oA-DFlrSGYpGsNPc18yik81vORRcSj6Pw/edit?pli=1&gid=0#gid=0] copy from original output (or similarly this [file|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1IMLDCHtWVpbUWx4xWuWBk7iYFsnUvkCkW3gso5ui4-U/edit?gid=1612750349#gid=1612750349])
* Running the models with weaker priors in Q3 would give the same result as in Q4 (i.e. we’ve bee keeping up good coefficients with priors exclusively) - see [here|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/editor/notebooks/2934471359379976?o=3829506390716583#command/2934471359380002]
** Interestingly, making the prior less informed did not change the situation for {{Google Android}} (vmax=36 vs vmax=41), meaning that priors did not play a huge role there.

*Paris*

* Original Q3 models for Paris all had the priors with {{sigma=50}}
* Having those same priors, but less informed ({{sigma=100}}) would:
** not really change Google Android {{vmax=354}} to {{vmax=359}}
** change vmax for all iOS channels by ~ 30% (from 300-ish to 200-ish)
** (Meaning that assessment of iOS performance could actually be a bit inflated)
* While modelling Q4, *vmax priors were also decreased* (which also contributed to us having lower coefficients):
** Google Android: 365 →  9 (probably under the influence of expiment)
** Google iOS 477 → 318
** Tiktok iOS 450 → 424
** Snapchat 93 → 44

*Berlin*

*Priors* in Berlin for Q4 models were also generally *decreased* (comparing [this|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/editor/notebooks/3292131742150652?o=3829506390716583#command/3292131742150678] notebook to results from spreadsheet, like in Paris):

* Google Android: 260 → 8
* Facebook Android: 170 →  182
* Tiktok Android: 187 → 39
* Google iOS: 287 → 94
* Facebook iOS:  172 → 109 
* Tiktok iOS:  565 → 440
* Snapchat iOS:  55 → 40

Running the Q3 notebook for Berlin with larger sigmas also generally led to decrease of vmax except 

* faceboook android (which actually increased)
* tiktok ios (which stayed almost the same)



This should be a signal for us to be more attentive on how we define prior sigmas (and how informed we want our priors to be).

For example, most of the priors for Germany were from {{#past model}}. Should we be using past model’s indication with some increased sigmas?

*Definition why here we take all error only for its random part*

* In this exercise, we cannot distinguish between random and bias (systematic error). However, we just take all the error and treat it as random just as a consideration for worst case scenario

*Adding random component - ways to do it and keeping the same language.*

-When we will be doing simulations, we will want to define the random component in terms of some total amount of signups (because error depends overall total level of signups). Therefore, we would like to define the error as signups*coefficient-

-There are two ways to do it as well:-

* -One way to add randomness is to add some error to each specific observation (error_i = signups_i)-
* -Other way to do it is calculate some average amount of signups and define all errors in relation to that number-

-Both ways are possible, it’s just important that we 1) define the error in simulations and 2) read it from actual markets as residuals in the same language.-

-So far, we just historically were simulating with the second approach, so to assess the uncertainty as residuals from the market we:-

* -first take the overall average over 1 year (avg(signups))-
* -calculate the residuals (prediction-model)-
** -take the std of residuals-
* -divide the std/total average-

-This will be the std that will be plugged in to np.random(std=..) param-



*NOTE: actually not really the same*

Decided that a more proper way is to actually:

* check what is the random noise in relation to signups on a very specific date (in percentage)
* calculate std of this percentage

This is because over the period signups can be different (e.g. smaller in spring, larger in summer). And we believe that error should be proportional to signups on each specific date (increase and decrease together with the trend).



*Also:*

Instead of  running one whole regression for  the period we ended up:

* running multiple regressions - for each city for each specific month (this gets us closer to error being actual error and not bias))
* relying on these regressions to for errors

Both points help to reduce the error by ~1-3pp, but I think it’s fair, because previous approaches would increase it to the scale that even visually does not look plausible.

Hi [~accountid:712020:53555a79-b384-46b1-8f21-2b13cb2c655a] 

From the gift card scheme described, I understand that it involves either the end-user or the B2B client of Amilon *purchasing* gift cards. This means that someone is making a prepayment for the gift cards. With this being the case, we have to treat this scheme as Bolt issuing a prepaid instrument, even if it is not directly Bolt who is receiving the prepayment from the buyer of the gift card. We cannot do this without a payment/e-money license. 

Regulatory authorities are likely to approach this scheme of purchasing a gift card/ digital code + applying the code in the Bolt app as one combined instrument (for which Bolt as issuer is ultimately liable). Even though Bolt itself would get paid only later for the redeemed codes, the value represented in the gift cards will be promised to the buyer of the gift card against prepayment from the buyer.

Theoretically it is possible, as also mentioned by Stefano, that such instruments may be issued without a license under the limited network licensing exclusion, but in our case, unfortunately we are limited in issuing similar payment instruments even under this licensing exclusion. Because for our main marketplace payments activity we need to be able to rely on the commercial agent licensing exemption, which allows us to strictly hold funds only for the seller side (the drivers/fleet) in our marketplace. Meaning that we should not issue prepaid payment instruments on the buyer side (to passengers). This is also why we have not enabled the user top up functionality of the Bolt Balance feature in our app in most of our markets. 

It is possible that other partners of Amilon are able to issue gift cards under similar scheme because they are not operating an intermediary platform business, meaning that unlike us they are also the sellers of the goods and services. Such instruments which are issued by the seller of goods and services are not considered regulated and can be provided without a license. Also some intermediary platform businesses may have obtained the relevant payment/e-money license.

Please let me know, if I have understood the setup accurately, or if I should clarify or further explain.

The question of possibility to apply discounts on orders containing alcohol as part of the Dine-Out feature should be considered from the perspective of provisions regulating the advertisement of alcoholic beverages in Poland.

+*Current legislation*+

Under Polish law the advertisement of alcoholic beverages, excluding beer, is strictly forbidden. Beer may be advertised provided that specific rules are observed. Currently, even though not explicitly specified in the definition of advertisement of alcoholic beverages, application of discounts can be qualified as such and therefore should not be allowed (again, except for beer). 

+*Fines*+ 

Advertisement or promotion of alcoholic beverages in violation of the above rules is threatened with a fine of up to PLN 500,000 (around EUR 120,000). Advertising contrary to the law may also be considered as an act of unfair competition and therefore theoretically infringement of consumer rights, which can be subject to a fine up to 10% turnover imposed by the Polish Office of Competition and Consumer Protection. Although we assess the chances of imposing fines by the latter as relatively low, they cannot be fully excluded.

+*Proposed changes to the legislation*+

There is a new legislative proposition that will expand the definition of the advertisement of alcoholic beverages (and, therefore, expand the list of prohibited advertising actions), including beer in the advertisement ban as well as qualifying sale of alcohol with discounts as an advertisement. I added Zuza from our public policy team to this ticket who has recently reviewed the draft law so that she can also take a look from her perspective.

+*Summary & recommendation*+

Taking the above into account, our recommendation would be that the discounted receipts include only beer. In that case, the banners advertising the Dine-Out option should include a disclaimer specifying that the discount will not apply on alcohol. 

In any case, should the proposed changes to the existing legislation and the expansion of the advertisement definition be introduced, discounts on any alcohol, including beer, will not be allowed at all.

Please let me know in case of any questions.

Hello everyone. They have accepted most of our suggestions, except the following two (in _italics_):

# *Clause 3, n.º 5 -* _With regard to fire safety obligations, the_ *_SECOND PARTY_* _confirms that the Property, in its condition on the date of this Contract, complies with all applicable legislation_.

* If they are not accepting, this may be an indicator that the Property, as is, may not be compliant. Compliance with fire safety regulations is usually necessary to obtain the license for use of the property. But, since this is a sublease and we are not leasing directly from the owner, I’m uncertain about how much reassurance about this we would be able to get from the landlord.
* Plus, the tenant is generally responsible for obtaining specific operational licenses required for their business, including any fire safety measures that relate to the specific activity - so we might even need to do some compliance with this ourselves, but I don’t know what are the demanded fire safety measures for office spaces.

# *Clause 6, n.º 6 -* The *SECOND PARTY* is solely responsible for the maintenance and upkeep of the property, and undertakes, at its own expense, to carry out all necessary repairs resulting from its own fault or negligence, with the exception of wear and tear caused by normal and prudent use, _being the_ *_FIRST PARTY_* _responsible for carrying out ordinary or extraordinary maintenance work, in accordance with article 1074.º, n.º 1 and article 1111.º of the Civil Code_

* I’m not to concerned about this, as I believe we are sufficiently covered by the applicable law. The responsibility for maintenance and repairs ultimately takes into consideration if the damage is caused by normal wear and tear, if it is caused by negligence or fault of the tenant, if it caused by external factors, etc. Plus, we have the protection of Clause 6, nº 2 and 3, that stipulates our possibility to report, after our possession of the property, any pre existing damages and their obligation to make all repairs, and our termination of the lease if they don’t comply.

# Additionally to this, prior to accepting Clause 6, n.º 4, they want to validate *Annex II* (which indicates all the work we want to do in the property). Do we already have a draft of this?

Hi team, 

If the pre-authorization fee exceeds 20% then an authorization adjustment is created. Adjustment is an action for incremental authorization. 

Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer. 
You can ask the customer to reach out to their bank in order to confirm the authorized funds have been released. Their bank can locate the funds with the authorization date and amount. 


Please let me know if you have any other questions.

Cheers,
Marten

Bolt have developed [Legal Contracting Standards|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/4039868417/Contract+Playbook+-+Bolt+Legal+Contracting+Standards] that are meant to be used as a uniform global guidance for Legal Counsels when reviewing any third-party contracts (including EHS). They should be used not only in relation to how we interpret clauses in third-party contracts but also in how we interpret feedback given to our templates (if any). We have also [Data Protection Contracting Playbook|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/LEG/pages/4499439674/Data+Protection+Contracting+Playbook] for information regarding the Data Processing Agreements (DPAs) where necessary. Any time there is a Legal SD ticket created this would be the main documents we would evaluate third-party contract against. Currently it provides guidance on following topics: [Warranties|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nbpYJMKM6XHQNMOEtUq-SuTaCI-lLPy_miKRH4btHyo/edit#heading=h.16r7zyzchlek], [Compliance with law|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nbpYJMKM6XHQNMOEtUq-SuTaCI-lLPy_miKRH4btHyo/edit#heading=h.vp13sa8j0ftw], [Confidentiality|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nbpYJMKM6XHQNMOEtUq-SuTaCI-lLPy_miKRH4btHyo/edit#heading=h.ashnyet3gnfw], [Publicity|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nbpYJMKM6XHQNMOEtUq-SuTaCI-lLPy_miKRH4btHyo/edit#heading=h.9tryogqlornw], [Intellectual Property Rights|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nbpYJMKM6XHQNMOEtUq-SuTaCI-lLPy_miKRH4btHyo/edit#heading=h.3kcu7meodx64], [Intellectual Property Indemnity|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nbpYJMKM6XHQNMOEtUq-SuTaCI-lLPy_miKRH4btHyo/edit#heading=h.ocywycv0qri], [Audit rights|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nbpYJMKM6XHQNMOEtUq-SuTaCI-lLPy_miKRH4btHyo/edit#heading=h.9vlruh9dvnt], [Limitation of Liability|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nbpYJMKM6XHQNMOEtUq-SuTaCI-lLPy_miKRH4btHyo/edit#heading=h.pq3ozfov4zzf], [Standard Indemnity (breach one-way - Customer to Supplier)|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nbpYJMKM6XHQNMOEtUq-SuTaCI-lLPy_miKRH4btHyo/edit#heading=h.c11r728lj456], [Change of Control|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nbpYJMKM6XHQNMOEtUq-SuTaCI-lLPy_miKRH4btHyo/edit#heading=h.s1d551hycykj], [Termination for Cause|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nbpYJMKM6XHQNMOEtUq-SuTaCI-lLPy_miKRH4btHyo/edit#heading=h.9w7idwp70wwq], [Termination for Convenience|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nbpYJMKM6XHQNMOEtUq-SuTaCI-lLPy_miKRH4btHyo/edit#heading=h.xvxzpxaoodxp], [Consequences of Termination|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nbpYJMKM6XHQNMOEtUq-SuTaCI-lLPy_miKRH4btHyo/edit#heading=h.uqrydyurr0jg], [Sub-contracting|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nbpYJMKM6XHQNMOEtUq-SuTaCI-lLPy_miKRH4btHyo/edit#heading=h.752ncy42hkdr], [Force Majeure|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nbpYJMKM6XHQNMOEtUq-SuTaCI-lLPy_miKRH4btHyo/edit#heading=h.vyrm3emxsqds], [Dispute Resolution|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nbpYJMKM6XHQNMOEtUq-SuTaCI-lLPy_miKRH4btHyo/edit#heading=h.bfuptlwprhma] and [Governing Law and Jurisdiction or Arbitration|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1nbpYJMKM6XHQNMOEtUq-SuTaCI-lLPy_miKRH4btHyo/edit#heading=h.jx7umqxzghgr]. These standards describes not only general intent and typical wording but also provides typical fallbacks. I would advise to use these documents to ensure a degree of consistency in our approach to EHS consultant contracts across different jurisdictions.

In addition to what is already described in the existing standards it would be good to define:

* Clear scope of work - specification of the precise tasks the consultant will perform. Include specific outcomes or deliverables (e.g., training programs, gap analyses, reports) along with deadlines or key milestones. Reference relevant standards (ISO 14001, ISO 45001, local EHS regulations) and clarity on the quality of work expected. If there is any local certifications required, consultant should have them.
* Compliance with the Law - it could be specified more in detail compared to the standards, for example, stating that the consultant must comply with all relevant local, national, and international EHS laws. We could also request that the consultant informs us in advance about any upcoming changes in EHS regulation in respective country so we stay ahead of it.
* Terms outlining how personal data, for example, employee health information will be handled, stored, and transferred, if it will be shared. Bolt Privacy team can support with this.
* Insurance requirements - require the consultant to maintain adequate professional liability coverage. 
* Reference to our internal EHS / sustainability policy (if any) so the consultant is aligned with our global values and approach.

If you as an EHS expert see any other topics that would be needed to be covered in such contracts, feel free to request it from the consultants.

We run 2 types of delivery fleet systems in the GH market; *Reseller fleet* and *Connector fleet.*

The reseller fleet type has fleets that have their own base of riders as employees of the fleet. The couriers under this setup have their delivery fees/ earnings sent to the fleet on a weekly basis and the fleet in turn pays those riders from the monies they have received from Bolt.

The connector fleet setup has fleets that accommodate independent riders that do not have their own courier license. These riders get their delivery fees paid out to them directly. However these riders have to pay a 2% commission on their weekly earnings to the fleets. So what happens is, every week, we calculate 2% of what the riders make on a weekly basis and pay that out to the connector fleet partner they fall under.

So this current fleet for which i raised this ticket is a connector fleet. Now they want to become a reseller fleet. I had the discussion with rides fraud team on repetitive business user - driver issue. And we have couple of solutions that would address this from the fraud side. 

1. Fraud team has number of profilings which can determine and flag the rides when a driver and rider has repetitive orders. I will not go into details but these profilings depend on a variety of data points that we receive into fraud engine. As of last year, postpaid business trips are excluded from those profilings based on the escalation from business local teams. My understanding is exclusion happened because especially in small regions companies tend to work with same drivers and flags from our side challenged those repetitions leading to complaints from the business user side.

Now how does those flags work and what could be the benefit of bringing them back for postpaid businesses? Flags by themselves do not take any actions except visually showing that match between a driver and a rider. In addition depending on the thresholds, flagged trips are also reviewed in driver payouts (earnings) - if suspicious fraud rides team reviews the trips involved and deny the payout for the drivers in case of fraud. 1. adding postpaid business to our profiling will help local ops or business team to have visuals over those orders. 2. they will also come up in driver payouts to be reviewed as a last step in the chain. 


# In addition to profilings, fraud engine can also block the involved drivers - depending on the number of repetitive trips they do with business accounts/or in case of regular trips as well. *_This process might be useful but given the results of our analysis repetitive orders are not a big issue with businesses - thus this would be too harsh of an approach to take for the product, potentially affecting good partners and customers._* There is also another development process in progress which will help us to move away from the hard blocking process in the near future. This means applying it for postpaid business would only be temporary and we would need to change the whole process with new development coming. 

Given that these are postpaid businesses fraud do not have extensive overviews over them however given these cases include driver fraud, above-mentioned solutions are the ones we can offer. And please let me know if you would be able to build any monitoring process over the repetitive orders or perhaps have something similar to be adjusted? This would help the local team to overview those orders/irregularities or spikes. 

Let me know what you think and we can proceed accordingly with the next steps from our side. 

Niki

Estimations on cluster upscale.

Currently we have 6*r6g.xlarge = 72Gb in total, $1,082/month

For 256Gb we need 23 such nodes, but 23 is not %3, so we need 24 of them, which increases costs by +$3,247/month to 4k. Total memory will be 24*12Gb=288Gb, next lower value is 21*12Gb=252Gb, costs diff +$2,706/month.

Out of other Graviton AWS ec2 instances, we can switch to x8g.xlarge * 12 instances, which has same 4 cores, but 64Gb of memory, diff in this case: +$3,759/month.

We can also use bigger r6g, which will bring lower amount of instances, keeping costs about the same (diff +$3,236/month), but restart time will be higher 2x. Now we estimated that recovery after restart on r6g.xlarge takes ~1 hour, so on bigger node it will take ~2h.

Only downside of having 24 smaller nodes is complexity in maintenance, but I think we should be fine with it. Smaller nodes also allow smaller iterations in upscale downscale, i.e. +/- 3 smaller nodes (3*12Gb) rather than (3*24Gb).

Hi Jo, thank you for reaching out and highlighting this concern.

I completely understand that safety issues can arise with cash rides, but turning off the cash rides option *would not address the root cause of the problem*. While disabling cash rides might reduce the risk for a particular driver, it wouldn't eliminate the underlying issues that contribute to these safety concerns.

Additionally, cash rides make up a significant portion of our GMV, and our team doesn’t have the authority to make a decision that would allow CS to actively promote the option for drivers to turn off cash rides, as this could lead to a substantial decline in orders. As I mentioned, while this measure may help reduce certain safety risks, it doesn't resolve the root causes. Our goal should be to address those issues directly and ensure all rides are safe, regardless of the payment method.

To summarize, the option to turn off cash rides is available to drivers, and they are aware of it. However, we won’t be able to advise CS to actively encourage this choice.

Please feel free to reach out if you have any further questions. Have a great day!

h3. *Overview*

The analysis covered a total of 280 tickets under three issue tags:

* *"I received a parking ticket"* (100 tickets)
* *"I received a fine for violating Bolt's T&Cs"* (100 tickets)
* *"I received a speeding ticket"* (80 tickets)

h3. *Findings by Issue Tag*

h4. *1. "I received a parking ticket"*

* *ATI Accuracy:* Only 3 cases had incorrect ATI selection, indicating high accuracy.
* *Unnecessary Escalations:* 4 cases were escalated to Local Ops despite all necessary information being available.
* *Quality Issues:* In 53 cases, responses lacked empathy, had poor structure, and contained insufficient information. This raises concerns about whether agents fully understand the process, as they struggled to clearly explain the fines.

h4. *2. "I received a fine for violating Bolt's T&Cs"*

* *ATI Accuracy Issues:*
** 7 tickets were assigned incorrect ATI:
*** 4 should have been tagged as "I received a speeding ticket."
*** 3 should have been "My account has been blocked."
* *Quality Issues:*
** 30 cases had poorly structured responses, failing to follow the building blocks guidelines.
** Some replies were passive-aggressive and lacked proper acknowledgment of the issue.
** Agents did not effectively educate users on fines and next steps.

h4. *3. "I received a speeding ticket"*

* *ATI Accuracy:*
** 2 tickets were incorrectly tagged.
* *Quality Issues:*
** 30 cases contained poor response structure, lacked empathy and had robotic or passive-aggressive tones.
** Agents did not sufficiently educate users on the process.

h3. *Key Trends & Recommendations*

h4. *1. Common User Concerns*

* *Multiple Fines Confusion:* 60% of cases involved users questioning why they must pay both an administrative Bolt fee and a municipal/police fine. While this is outlined in the Terms & Conditions, adding an FAQ would be beneficial, because it creates a huge confusion, about what are these penalties. Also, in Germany, our fee is 30 euro and the penalty from the police in some situations is 20 eur. (Example - [ticket 1|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/505336445], [ticket 2|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/502488012], [ticket 3|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/467330474]).
* *Lack of Awareness Among Agents:* Many agents appear unaware of administrative fees and struggle to explain them properly (Example - [ticket 1|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/525644334], [ticket 2|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/524704356], [ticket 3|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/513397937]).
* *Redundant Issue Tags:*
** The three ATI categories may not be necessary, as most cases under "I received a parking ticket" and "I received a fine for violating Bolt’s T&Cs" involve the same queries.
* *Missing Fee Information:* The administrative fee amount is not listed in the KB article, making it difficult for agents to provide complete answers.

h4. *2. Handling Evidence Requests*

* Some users request evidence of the violation.
* Agent responses were inconsistent:
** Some stated that the information could not be shared and that the fine would be sent via mail/post. ([ticket 1|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/524051369]).
** Others provided the document via Beehive or escalated to the Ops team ([ticket 1|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/502652964], [ticket 2|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/487275319], [ticket 3|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/524150347], [ticket 4|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/523838518], [ticket 5|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/517284943]).
* A standardized response and clear policy on evidence-sharing should be established.

h4. *3. Payment Issues*

* Users often struggle to pay fines due to insufficient balance on their linked card.
* They then face difficulties adding a new payment method ([Ticket 1|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/526000977]).
* This information is missing from the KB and should be clearly explained, including:
** How Bolt processes payments.
** Whether the full amount can be paid through the app or if users must make separate payments.

h4. *4. Clarifying the Fine Process*

* Users frequently contact support after receiving a speed camera fine, asking about the next steps ([ticket 1|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/476444180], [ticket 2|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/491390061], [ticket 3|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/506292357]).
* Agents provide inconsistent responses.
* A step-by-step guide in the KB article would help standardize replies and reduce confusion.

Hi Matilda,

For drivers with active email access, we can follow the standard procedure. However, for those who lack access due to forgotten passwords or inactivity, we implement a modified approach.

Specifically, for drivers without email access, we will:

* Initiate the account change process at the Driver Engagement Center.
* Ensure the driver confirms access to the new email address on their device _before_ finalizing any changes.

The primary driver behind this modified process is GDPR compliance. We require documented, written consent from drivers for all account modifications. This serves as crucial evidence, protecting us in situations where a driver might later dispute the change, especially if the employee involved is no longer available. This written confirmation, obtained at the engagement center, reinforces verbal consent and provides a clear audit trail.

Number of Users: 188

Organisations can purchase additional bundles of credits as required if they consume all the credits provided upfront, but we are yet to see that happen! I checked with OKAI whether IOT uses the battery detection sensor for re-sending any commands if some conditions are not met, but OKAI responded conclusively that IOT does not send any battery unlock commands without instructions (command from BE), and the battery induction sensor is just a value which is sent to backend. They also mentioned that the detection system is often inaccurate, making it unreliable as a source of information. This means that any analysis we have done, we can’t use it as actionable data as broken sensors or bad design of sensor causes false positives.

!image-20250319-135524.png|width=1634,height=799,alt="image-20250319-135524.png"!

So far, we have checked cases together with Keijo and Kaido upon reports from the local team, which have resulted in no conclusions:

* the vehicle logs show no command being sent to the vehicle and vehicle not sending any other status messages indicating that battery detection has changed (No +RESP:GTMLS)
* the Kibana logs (Charger app input) does not show anything indicating towards a command being buffered 



My suggestion is to proceed as follows and keep monitoring cases where online vehicles at the WH are locks are supposedly opening and releasing batteries and note down the unlocking time to see if we notice anything peculiar. The weird thing is that I we’ve had EB100, ES400 and ES600 vehicles in HQ with different HW/FW versions and different lock versions, and we have *never encountered a battery popping out on its own*.

Ideally we would check vehicles with known often occurrences and snoop the CANBUS to see if we can see any activity there. If we can find such vehicle that does this more often than others, then should consult with OKAI to check whether on the CANBUS there are commands being sent.

To give you some context, the amendment to the Act on Upbringing in Sobriety and Counteracting Alcoholism, which regulates among others verification of consumers and promotional activities, has been in preparation since Q3 2024. The Ministry of Health who is responsible for the bill is determined to amend the current legislation, having previously announced willingness to *ban online alcohol sales entirely.* Following industry-wide mitigating activities, this proposition was not included in the amendment, however the MoH expressed willingness to further regulate the sector in the future. 

Currently, the legislative proposal focuses on: 

#  *Restriction of alcoholic beverage promotion* - expanding the definition of alcoholic beverage promotion, including beer in the promotion ban, eliminating the promotional exception for designated sales areas.
# *Protection of consumer safety* - introducing requirements for alcoholic beverage packaging (material, appearance), prohibiting the sale of alcohol in forms other than liquid.
# *Tightening sales regulations* - introducing an obligation to refuse sale in case of failure to present an age verification document, increasing penalties for illegal promotional activities.

*Proposed changes with regards to promotion of alcoholic beverages:*

a) Promotion of alcoholic beverages - public tasting of alcoholic beverages, distribution of items related to alcoholic beverages, organization of premium sales of alcoholic beverages, sale of alcoholic beverages with discounts, rebates, bonuses, loyalty packages and programs, donations, prizes, trips, games of chance, mutual betting, all forms of lending, tied transactions, all types of vouchers and coupons, and providing other *unspecified financial or personal benefits for the purchaser of alcoholic beverages*, as well as other forms of publicly encouraging the purchase of alcoholic beverages.

b) The amendments proposed in the provisions of section 13(1) (Article 1 point 4 of the bill) of the Act are aimed at standardising the possibility of promoting all alcoholic beverages, by supplementing the general rule prohibiting the promotion of alcoholic beverages with the promotion of beer. 

*Currently, the legislative proposal is undergoing public consultations which will last until mid-April. The planned approval by the Council of Ministers is Q3 2025, and entry into force is planned for January 1st, 2026.* 

The Ministry of Health is highly motivated to have this bill approved. On top of that, many big cities have already implemented or are considering the implementation of night time prohibition of alcohol sale - to paint you a picture of the sentiment towards alcohol sale, especially among activists and left-wing politicians.

*What if a customer itself wants to see this reflected in the agreement?*

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Same feature as raised on [+LSS-47190+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-47190]. 
* Advice was as follows:
** *Risk*: May be seen as intrusive by riders.
*** *Mitigations*: (1) Limit live sharing to a specific period (this is already enabled, as it only happens from 2 minutes to the pickup location; (2) Give riders control over whether their real-time location is shared (this is already enabled, as riders can opt-out); (3) Prove that this feature has been considered and is proportionate (a LIA (IMO legitimate interest is the best legal basis here, since the feature is enabled by default and benefits both drivers and passengers) and a DPIA would help here).
** *Risk*: May be seen as invisible processing / may come as a surprise to riders.
*** *Mitigations*: Ensure proper transparency materials are in place. This includes: (1) clear guidance on the feature (which is apparently already enabled through a modal screen); and (2) updates to the passenger privacy notice (which is mostly there already, but the row titled _To enable, improve and customise the transportation services and other services/features by connecting Passengers with Drivers_ does not list legitimate interest as a legal basis).
** *Risk*: If we retain this data beyond for too long, this may be regarded as disproportionate. Also, riders may request this data as a DSAR, which we are not equipped for.
*** *Mitigations*: To sidestep these issues, I think we should just delete the data as standard from our systems once the rider has been picked up.
** *Conclusion*: Green-light this feature, subject to the following:
*** Advice to the business:
**** Ensure the rider location data is deleted from our systems once the rider has been picked up, unless there is a pressing need to retain it for longer.
*** Actions from the Privacy Team (not a blocker):
**** If one has not already been prepared, then draft a LIA and DPIA for this.
**** Update the Passenger Privacy Notice per the above.

+*ANALYSIS*+

* This is not directly relevant to the ICO investigation, so fine from that POV.
* Advice is not substantially different for UK POV. Other things to consider:
** We could rely on consent here, particularly as the modal screen actively asks the rider to ‘share’. Also, looks like the rider could revoke the consent at any time. However, looks like the rider can only opt-out when a ride is live.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Check whether this is opt-in or enabled by default.
* In any case, low risk and no substantive comments. Green-light with usual recommendations.

Hi [~accountid:6332c7ab409249995ee9c5e8] - I have taken a look at this from a Privacy POV and include my thoughts below.

{panel:bgColor=#e3fcef}
*In short:* We can *go ahead* with this from a Privacy POV *_provided that_*:

* We are using the same model screen / opt-out functionality as is currently used in other jurisdictions (I have a question on this further below re opting in - please take a look at this); and
* We are not retaining data on the rider’s live location for any longer than is necessary (ideally, we should delete it immediately unless there is a pressing need to retain it).

On our side, we will need to update the Privacy notice and complete some back-end compliance documentation, but these action items should not act as blockers to pushing ahead.
{panel}

More detailed analysis is below, for context.

*Opting out*

I understand that this feature is enabled by default -{color:#4c9aff} *are we certain this is the case, rather than being opt-in*{color}? Based on the modal screen that I was shown on [+LSS-47190+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-47190], it looks like the rider is opt-in in to sharing their live location, rather than this being enabled by default. Could you please clarify?
If it is enabled by default (i.e., not opt-in), this is a position that we can defend, provided that it is quick and easy for riders to opt out. I just want to check this to confirm my understanding.

*Transparency*

We need to make sure that riders are fully aware of this feature, and are sufficiently informed about what it entails. The modal screen appears to cover this, so we need to make sure this is also used for implementation in the UK.
We will need to make some adjustments to the Passenger Privacy Notice, but these do not act as a blocker for now.

*Retention of location information*

We need to make sure at all times that we are limiting the processing of live location data to what is strictly necessary. I understand that we only start collecting such data 2 minutes from the pickup location - this is good to hear. In addition, we should apply the same principles to *_storing_* the location data that we have collected in this context (i.e., not retaining it for any longer than we need to).
Unless there is a pressing / legal reason to do so (which I am currently unaware of), ideally we should *delete the rider’s live location data immediately after the trip*, and not retain it for any longer. This would allow us to sidestep a lot of the privacy issues associated with collecting such data - in particular, we would not need to provide this data to a rider if they asked for a copy (which would incur time and resources). {color:#4c9aff}*Is the plan currently to do this?*{color}

Hi Team, while I appreciate the trust you put into me in this topic, as I’ve said in other instances I am not a Fire Protection Specialist, a Fire Safety Expert, or a lawyer, thus cannot provide detailed guidance in the topic, so please treat below as general idea, not law interpretation or guidance.

From non-fire experts POV we could assume that, as IBP has been prepared by someone with necessary qualifications it is correct. However failure to have an up-to-date IBP (Instrukcja Bezpieczeństwa Pożarowego) (f.e. missing key info about storing and charging batteries) can result in the imposition of a financial penalty by the authorities of the State Fire Service, or in the facility not being allowed to be used, and in the event of a fire outbreak in the absence of compensation payments by insurance companies. Polish regulations leave lots of room for interpretation on who is responsible for updating IBP, some say it’s the building owner (landlord), other that the actual user (Bolt) is responsible for that. For all future contract I’d implement requirement that landlord is required to prepare and maintain IBP, and equip location according to it. As [~accountid:712020:3c6c8d76-7a41-4491-a752-76e034e2c39a] has said - potential liabilities come to the fact if we’re able to prove that landlord at the moment of updating IBP has been aware of the amount of the batteries, workshop chemicals, etc. that we’re storing and using in this location.

*Status update*: 
The NIS2 Directive has not yet been transposed into Estonian law. Estonia has already introduced fairly comprehensive cybersecurity provisions in its *Cybersecurity Act* and it will be supplemented by the provisions set out in NIS2. The existing Cybersecurity Act largely regulate cybersecurity requirements in line with the NIS2 Directive. Pursuant to the draft law, planned date for entry into force of the national law, transposing the NIS2 Directive, is *July 1, 2025*. As of entry into force of the law transposing the NIS2 Directive, obliged companies will have *3 years* to comply with cybersecurity requirements.

*What is LT OPS reason for the attached process? Do they want to give extra responsibility to CS? Are the volumes high?*
We would like to avoid Uber-branded vehicles operating on the Bolt platform and take immediate action when informed by a rider, driver, or any other individual. CS agents should be more involved in these cases, as the verification process is straightforward. The current volume of such cases is low, as Uber has only recently started branding their vehicles in Lithuania. However, we need to be prepared for a potential increase in the number of branded vehicles.

Additionally, the process differs as we provide the driver with an appropriate timeframe to complete the de-branding of the vehicle.

*Why can’t CS contact the driver from the ticket the rider sent us? Why are Step 1 and Step 2 necessary?*
The report of an Uber-branded vehicle can come from various sources—not only from a rider but also from another driver or any individual who notices a branded vehicle on the street. They may inquire whether the vehicle is listed on the Bolt platform. Therefore, Step 1 and Step 2 are necessary to ensure proper verification. If a rider contacts CS, the agent will verify the driver through the order details.

*What photo are we referring to in Step 2?*
The photo in Step 2 should clearly show the Uber-branded vehicle along with its license plate, which can then be verified in the Admin system.

*What is considered proof? Drivers could send outdated photos of their cars before the competitor branding was applied…*
To prevent the submission of outdated photos, we require drivers to include a white A4 paper with the current date written on it in the photo. This measure ensures authenticity, as any attempt to manipulate the image using Photoshop would be easily detectable.

*Which designated sheet?*
[This sheet|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1ET8NNFmgaP0orGxV68GFm5lbMKOOAZSfiQkY_q5uKrc/edit?gid=719837815#gid=719837815].

*Is the template a legal requirement? We would rather not use a template if it’s not a legal requirement. We can just instruct agents to inform drivers that branding their cars with competitors’ stickers is against our T&C.*
Template is prepared using the legal clarification. This approach has been legally approved, as legal has advised providing the driver with a designated period for de-branding.

*What are the expected volumes?*
Uber began branding their vehicles in Lithuania only a few months ago, so the current volumes are low. However, we must be prepared for a potential increase.
